Does Audapter do what experimenters think it does? An audit of the blab-lab version

By
Claude (Anthropic), at the request of Josh Mandel
Code examined
blab-lab/audapter_mex @169cadf and blab-lab/audapter_matlab @e1695f1
Date
2026-09-27

What we looked at

Audapter shifts a speaker's formants or pitch, or plays masking noise, in real time for altered-auditory-feedback experiments. We examined the blab-lab version, its C++ core and MATLAB code, and asked: does it do what experimenters think it does, trial after trial?

How

  • We ran the real code without MATLAB or audio hardware, fed it synthetic voices and 80 real voice recordings, and measured what came out (method).
  • We checked for memory errors with standard sanitizers, and simulated the live sound-card path, including its two threads.
  • We proved a few pieces of logic correct or incorrect for all settings.
  • A browser build lets you rerun several findings on this page, with and without a fix.

What we found

The core works: formant shifts deliver what they log, and pitch shifts land within a few cents of what was asked.

No blab experiment we inspected is exposed to trial-to-trial carry-over. We checked the OST files and the way conditions are switched between trials in 10 public blab experiments and in blab's unpublished experiment code (including timeWrap, pitchAdaptPD and pitchComp). None uses the settings that let one trial's state leak into the next, and in simulated mixed sessions with the lab's settings, catch trials received no perturbation whatever came before them (details).

What does touch current experiments:

  • Masking noise drops out. In the many blab runners that load the noise once per session, since b2.4 (April 2026) the bundled babble goes silent for 16 ms about every 10 s of running time: in about 1 in 5.6 trials of a masking phase. Data collected before April 2026 are not affected (I-01).
  • A loudness and latency step in two time-warp studies. In timeWrap and cerebTimeAdapt the pre phase runs with the phase vocoder off and later phases in its time-warp mode, so from the first phase after pre onward participants hear their own voice 2.8–3.5 dBA quieter and 13 ms later. The timeAdapt family plays at -0.3 dBA (PT-5).
  • Formant shifts change the level. blab's MATLAB defaults switch off Audapter's gain adaptation, so a formant shift also changes the heard level: on real voices, lowering F1 by 125 mel raised it by a median 2.9 dBA (1.3 to 2.8 phon by the ISO 532-1 loudness model on two voices), enough to notice, and raising F1 changed it by a median -1.4 dBA. Shifted and unshifted trials therefore differ in loudness in every blab formant study (FMT-LEVEL).
  • vsaSentence depends on an undocumented blab change. The field perturbation switches on again at every vowel; on the original Audapter 2.1.5 or another fork, only the first vowel of each sentence would be perturbed (F6).
  • One open question about the public vsaGeneralize runner. As committed, it perturbs the baseline trials and never scales the field (LAB-2); its experiment script calls it, and the lab's logs can settle it. The later vsaGeneralize2 study is wired correctly. Two smaller notes: vsaCentralize's repository ships an unused, mis-wired runner (LAB-1), and vsaGeneralize's p.fb4Gain line has no effect, as the lab's code already notes (LAB-3).

Pitfalls for future designs. Carry-over is real with other settings: an offset rule placed after a timer or after the RMS-floor rule fires later on every trial (OST-F1); a PCF left loaded overrides a later field experiment (COORD-1); pitch catch trials made by clearing the PCF can be shifted (OST-F5). Each card gives the safe pattern. Other pitfalls include wrongly logged pitch for low voices with time-domain shifting, crashes or hangs when settings change mid-session, and clicks when resetting during speech (all).

Robustness. A few memory errors need a malformed file or array to show up (all).

None of these produce a warning. Most cards include a fix you can try on this page.

Reading a card

Each card says what happens, when it matters, and gives an example with the exact settings it used (from a named blab experiment where one exists), a figure, recordings, the size of the effect, the cause, the safe pattern or fix, and the evidence. Figures show two aligned panels: Expected, what the design should do, and Observed, what Audapter did. Grey boxes are the spoken words, outlined blocks are the intended perturbation, solid blue blocks are the perturbation Audapter applied, and orange marks the difference. Numbers under the words are measured on the audio you can play, not taken from Audapter's logs.

What affects blab's current experiments

These findings touch experiments the lab runs now, with the lab's own settings: a masking-noise defect introduced with b2.4 in April 2026, a loudness and latency step between phases in two time-warp studies, and a blab change that one of the lab's designs depends on.

I-01

High severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

Since b2.4 (April 2026), masking noise drops out for 16 ms about once every 10 s, in about one of every five or six trials of a blab masking phase

Affects blab's current experiments on b2.4 and later.
Relevant blab studies affected. Affected, on data collected with b2.4 or later (since April 2026) only: runners that load the noise once per session, so its position runs on across trials. Public: simonSingleWord v2, v1, coAdapt, simonMultisyllable v2, attentionComp, attentionAdapt, uhdapter, vsaCentralize (its committed experiment script calls a runner that is not in the repository), vsaGeneralize, vsaSentence, the free-speech template (each link is the line that loads the noise once). Unpublished: timeAdapt, timeWrap, varMod, sponAdapt, vsaRetention, diphthongAdapt, brut, vin, and the simon and cerebellar studies. Safe as run: runners that reload the noise before every trial, which rewinds it (the MRI and iEEG interleaved runners, noGoAdapt, varModAdapt, compRetest). How audible: in fb 3 (most runners; babble at gain 0.02 under the participant's own voice) a 16 ms dropout is subtle; fb 2 studies (brut, vin, and the masking phases of simonSingleWord v2, uhdapter and vsaSentence) and fb 4 studies (vsaGeneralize, biteblockAdapt, diphthongAdapt, sponAdapt, sponAdapt2, vsaRetention) are more exposed, because the noise is all or most of what is heard.

What happens

In feedback modes 2–5 Audapter plays the loaded noise (datapb) in a loop. It loops at the end of its 480,000-sample (10 s) buffer, not at the end of the noise that was loaded, and the unused end of the buffer is silence. The bundled babble is 479,230 samples, 770 short of the buffer, so once per 10 s of running time the participant hears 16 ms of silence instead of noise. The noise position carries on from trial to trial (reset does not rewind it), so the dropout lands at a different point in each affected trial. A noise file much shorter than 10 s gives a correspondingly longer silence.

When it matters

Matters whenever masking noise is meant to be continuous, most of all in fb 2 masking phases (transfer or noise-baseline phases), where the noise is all the participant hears and a dropout briefly unmasks their own voice. In fb 3 phases the babble is quiet (fb3Gain 0.02) and a 16 ms dropout is less noticeable. Safe if the loaded noise is exactly 480,000 samples, or on versions before b2.4.

Example

The masking phase of blab's simonSingleWord v2 experiment (fb 2, fb2Gain 0.16, 1.8 s trials, AudapterIO('init') every trial, the bundled babble loaded once with get_noiseSource). Over 24 trials the current build plays 4 silences of 16 ms, in trials 6, 12, 17, 23, at 0.98 s, 0.18 s, 1.18 s, 0.38 s into the trial. With the pre-b2.4 buffer the same session plays none.

Run it in your browser

The general case, beyond the bundled babble: a noise file shorter than 10 s. This runs a 12 s trial through the real Audapter C++ core compiled to WebAssembly from the pinned commit, once as released and once with the noise looping at the length that was loaded. Both builds keep the shipped 480000-sample playback buffer. Pick the length of the noise file, cut from the bundled babble and loaded as runExperiment.m does it (zero mean, unit RMS). The page ships only every third sample of the babble, the only samples the fb 2–5 loop reads, and rebuilds the 48 kHz buffer from them, so Audapter reads the same values it would read from the full-rate file. The bars come from a noise-only run (fb 2), and Play gives the voice + noise run (fb 3). Both use the 48 kHz output Audapter returns for every frame, which lags signalOut by a few milliseconds. The build used here records only 10 s, so its signalOut would not cover a 12 s trial.

The change in the “fix-i-01” build: report/patches/i-01-datapb-loop-length.patch
Audapter.cpppbLen               = maxPBSize;    /* audit fix I-01 */pbLen = (len > 0) ? len : maxPBSize;    /* audit fix I-01: loop at the loaded length */if (pbCounter >= maxPBSize)pbCounter -= maxPBSize;if (pbCounter >= pbLen) /* audit fix I-01: was maxPBSize */pbCounter -= pbLen;Audapter.hint pbLen;  /* audit fix I-01: length of the loaded datapb (loop point) */

Each run loads the Audapter core in this page, about 150–300 MB of memory per build. On a phone, run one panel at a time. Try your own recordings and settings in the Playground.

Data: data.json from the export script.

Cause

The fb 2–5 loop advances pbCounter and wraps it at the compile-time maxPBSize. Setting datapb zero-fills the rest of the buffer, and only setting datapb resets pbCounter.

Only since blab b2.4 (commit 3c90a3a, 6 April 2026), which enlarged the playback buffer from 230,400 to 480,000 samples. Data collected with earlier versions are not affected: the bundled babble was truncated to the old buffer and looped seamlessly.

Workaround and fix

Workarounds for current sessions (any one): (1) reload the noise with Audapter('setParam', 'datapb', w, 1) before each trial, which rewinds it, as blab's per-trial runners do (a trial then never reaches the 10 s loop point); (2) pad or trim the noise to exactly 480,000 samples before loading it, for example by appending the bundled babble's own first 770 samples; (3) apply the loop-at-length patch below. This applies only to data collected with b2.4 or later (since April 2026). Fix: store the loaded length when datapb is set and wrap there (report/patches/i-01-datapb-loop-length.patch), and rewind pbCounter in reset(). Check past data: if signalOut was saved for fb 2–5 trials, look for runs of exact zeros; otherwise the gap's position can be reconstructed from the trial durations, since the noise position runs on across trials.

  • H public experiments run with their own scripts (labrun): labrun/README.md LABRUN-3, VOICES-2: 15.4 ms holes every 10.0 s of noise running time in the modelExpt (9–12) and vsaGeneralize (22–34) full sessions with eight AI-generated voices (holes under the voice are not counted)
  • H real session structure: exp_noise_session.m EXP-3: 4 gaps of 16 ms in 24 trials on the current build, none with the pre-b2.4 buffer
  • H report export (generic case, a 5 s noise file): report_i01.m

PT-5

High severity

  • H Harness
  • D Driver
  • F Formal

Audit notes
Findings log

In blab's timeWrap and cerebTimeAdapt, participants hear their own voice 2.8–3.5 dBA quieter and 13 ms later from the first phase after pre onward, because the later phases switch the phase vocoder into its time-warp mode

Affects designs whose phases differ in how the phase vocoder runs: off in a baseline and in warp mode later (timeWrap, cerebTimeAdapt), on without a PCF, or with the warp section dropped on some trials.
Relevant blab studies affected. Affected: timeWrap and cerebTimeAdapt (24 kHz, frameLen 32, nDelay 3; pre phase with bPitchShift 0 and no PCF, later phases with bPitchShift 1 and a warp-row PCF; both experiment scripts call the Audapter runner for both phases). Measured at those settings the voice is played 0.0 dBA in the pre phase and -2.8 dBA afterwards on this sentence (-3.5 to -2.8 dBA across 4 voices), and 13.3 ms later. The timeAdapt family (frameLen 48) plays at -0.3 dBA with its warp rows. No blab study we know of uses the vocoder without a PCF (part C).

What happens

With bPitchShift = 1 the phase vocoder processes the voice even at 0 semitones. Without a time-warp section in the PCF, it plays the voice louder than it came in: +3.5 dBA at the default 16 kHz / frameLen 32, and +6.0 dBA at the 24 kHz / frameLen 48 settings blab uses for time warping. With a warp section loaded, even a zero-length one, the vocoder runs in its warp mode for the whole trial, at a different level: -0.3 dBA at 24 kHz / frameLen 48, -2.6 dBA at 16 kHz / frameLen 32. When a pitch shift starts, the level changes again, by an amount that depends on F0 and vowel.

When it matters

Matters when trials or phases differ in whether a warp section is loaded (a loudness cue that tells the participant which trials are perturbed), when the vocoder is on in some phases and off in others (for example a calibration at bPitchShift = 0), and for pitch-shift onsets. Safe if every trial carries a warp section (a zero-length row on control trials), as in blab's timeWrap experiment.

Example

A. timeWrap and cerebTimeAdapt. Their settings on a real sentence: in the pre phase (bPitchShift 0, no PCF) the voice is played at 0.0 dBA; in the later phases (bPitchShift 1, a PCF with a warp row, here zero-length as on a control trial) at -2.8 dBA, with a real warp at -2.8 dBA. On 4 voices the step is -3.5 to -2.8 dBA. The output also comes later: clicks sent through the same path arrive 2.7 ms after the input in the pre phase and 16.0 ms after it in the later phases, a 13.3 ms step at the phase boundary. B. Time-warp designs at timeAdapt settings (24 kHz, frameLen 48): if control trials keep a zero-length warp row, both kinds play at the spoken level (control -0.3 dBA, warp -0.2 dBA); if control trials drop the warp section, they play at +6.0 dBA, 6.2 dBA louder than the warp trials around them. C. A plausible design, not one blab runs: the vocoder on without a PCF after a baseline with it off (24 kHz, frameLen 32, nDelay 3) plays 0.0 dBA then +3.5 dBA. Clearing a warp PCF with Audapter('pcf', '', 0) leaves the vocoder in its warp mode for the rest of the MATLAB session: at the part-C settings a no-PCF trial run after warp trials plays at -2.8 dBA instead of +3.5 dBA, so the level of a later phase depends on what ran earlier in the session.

Run it in your browser

The pitch-onset part of this finding: a sustained /a/ at 120 Hz whose PCF steps from 0 to +2 semitones at 0.6 s (16 kHz defaults). This runs that trial through the real Audapter C++ core compiled to WebAssembly from the pinned commit, once as released and once with the overlap-add normalised. Pick the size of the step. Each trace is the output's RMS level in 20 ms blocks relative to the same input run with bPitchShift = 0, so 0 dB is the level a participant should hear.

The change in the “fix-pt-5” build: report/patches/pt-5-ola-normalise.patch
phase_vocoder.cpp/* audit fix PT-5: Hann analysis x Hann synthesis overlap-added at hop = L/osamp sums to 3*osamp/8, so with the2/(osamp/2) factor below the output is 1.5 x the input (+3.52 dB) for any osamp >= 4. Divide it out in pitch-shiftmode. dBA: the A-weighted level difference, measured on the audio. Phon: model estimates (ISO 532-1, Zwicker) for a normal-hearing listener on headphones with a flat response, the expected clip presented at 60, 70, 80 and 85 dB SPL (A-weighted) and the observed clip at the same gain. Plain RMS: the unweighted level difference, for reference. Older or clinical listeners and real headphones may differ. Part A is a pure gain change (same spectrum), so the model adds little to the level figure there; the pitch onset moves energy up in frequency, where equal-loudness contours differ, so level and loudness can differ. How this is computed.

Data: data.json from the export script.

Cause

Analysis and synthesis both use a Hann window with a hop of a quarter frame. Overlap-adding the squared window sums to 1.5, and the synthesis scaling does not divide this out, so the output is 1.5 times the input at any shift ratio (2 times at frameLen 48, measured; we have not located the extra factor in the code, EXP-11). Once a PCF has a warp section, the vocoder runs in its time-warp mode for the whole trial, and that mode has a different gain (measured, COORD-4). With a shift, each frequency bin is resynthesised with fresh phase, so the level then depends on the signal. The normalisation switch is registered under a misspelt name, and its code divides by a quantity that is always zero.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Safe pattern and fix

Safe pattern: in a warp design, give every trial a warp section, a zero-length one on control trials, as blab's timeWrap experiment does; then all trials play at the same level. Calibrate loudness with the vocoder in the mode the experiment uses, not with bPitchShift = 0. Fix: divide the pitch-shift overlap-add by its actual window sum. report/patches/pt-5-ola-normalise.patch divides by 1.5, which gives unity gain at frameLen 32 and 64; at frameLen 48 the sum is 2, and the patch leaves +2.5 dB (checked in the browser build). A shift still changes the level, which needs a running level match. Fixing only the parameter name is not safe (the code then outputs NaN).

How we know

  • H harness test: t_pitch.m FAIL “pvoc: unity gain at 0 st”: gain 3.52 dB
  • H harness test: t_pitch.m FAIL “pvoc: no loudness step 0 -> +2 st”: step -3.15 dB
  • H report export + F0/vowel sweep: report_pt5.m
  • D standalone pvoc driver: scratch/pitch-time/pv_test.cpp gain 1.500 at 0 st on pure tones
  • F exact algebra on the Hann window: formal/ola/ola_exact.py the 0 st overlap-add gain is exactly 3/2 (+3.52 dB) for every hop ratio pvocFrameLen/pvocHop of 3 or more, independent of frame length, hop and sample rate; the unity fix is a factor 2/3 at phase_vocoder.cpp:467 (FORMAL-7)
  • F the real phase_vocoder.cpp, measured: formal/ola/pv_gain.cpp 1.5000 at hop ratios 4 and 8; content below the first bin gets 5/2; at hop ratio 2 the gain swings between 1 and 2 at the hop rate

Reproduce cd audit/harness && ./run-oct.sh t_pitch.m

FMT-LEVEL

Medium severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

With gain adaptation off, as in every blab formant experiment, a formant shift changes the heard level: on real voices, lowering F1 by 125 mel raised it by a median +2.9 dBA and raising it changed it by a median -1.4 dBA, so perturbed trials carry a level cue

Affects formant-shift experiments run with bGainAdapt 0, which is what getAudapterDefaultParams sends.
Relevant blab studies affected. Affected: every blab formant experiment, because getAudapterDefaultParams sets p.gainAdapt = 0 and AudapterIO('init') always sends it; no blab runner changes it. The level goes with the condition: attentionComp's shifted trials are louder than its noShift (catch) trials (shiftIH, F1 down, by -0.0 to 2.6 dBA; shiftAE, F1 up and F2 down, by 0.4 to 2.2 dBA, across voices); coAdapt's down-shifted word is louder than its up-shifted word; in simonSingleWord the level changes where the shift direction flips inside "bedhead". The 2-D centralization fields at strength 0.5 (the VSA studies) change the level by -1.8 to +0.7 dBA.

What happens

Audapter's formant shifter moves the two lowest resonances with a pair of filters. Moving a resonance changes how much of the voice's energy passes through, so the output level changes with the shift (in our runs, up when F1 is lowered, with exceptions such as a sustained /i/ with a very low F1; raising F1 changes it less and in either direction). Audapter has a gain-adaptation step that computes the filters' gain change and divides it out (bGainAdapt), but the MATLAB defaults switch it off. With it off, the level of every shifted trial differs from an unshifted trial of the same speech, by an amount that depends on the direction and size of the shift and on the vowel.

When it matters

Matters for designs that compare shifted and unshifted trials (compensation designs with catch trials) or opposite shifts (up vs down), because the level difference goes with the condition, and for any analysis of produced loudness after a shift. For reference, a level change of about 1 dB is noticeable in broadband sounds such as speech (Miller 1947). Natural speech has the opposite tendency (open vowels with high F1 are intrinsically louder), so the cue is also unnatural. Lowering F1 mostly boosts the strong low harmonics, to which the ear is less sensitive, so the heard change is smaller than the unweighted level suggests: on the two ARCTIC voices whose clips are below, the loudness model gives +1.3 to +2.8 phon for F1 −125 mel and -1.8 to -1.2 phon for F1 +125 mel (ISO 532-1, 60–85 dB SPL). With bGainAdapt 1 the cue does not go away but reverses: gain adaptation equalises the unweighted level, so the heard level then drops when F1 is lowered (median -1.4 dBA, -3.2 to -1.4 phon on the two ARCTIC voices) and rises when it is raised (median +2.4 dBA). Switching it on is not a simple fix.

Example

Eight real voices (four ARCTIC sentences, two PVQD speakers' sustained /a/ and /i/), each shifted and unshifted with the same settings (blab defaults, field mode, fb 1 so the voice can be measured). On the ARCTIC bdl sentence: F1 −125 mel +2.9 dBA, F1 +125 mel -0.7 dBA, F1 −20 % +1.2 dBA, F1 +20 % -0.4 dBA, 2-D centralization +0.7 dBA, re the unshifted output over the shifted span. Running the public coAdapt and attentionComp experiments with their own scripts, spoken by 8 AI-generated voices (heard level = signalOut × dScale re input), shows level differences by condition within one phase: coAdapt's down-shifted word is 0.5–5.4 dBA (median 2.9) louder than its up-shifted word, and attentionComp's shiftIH and shiftAE trials are up to 2.6 and 2.2 dBA louder than its catch trials.

dBA: the A-weighted level difference, measured on the audio. Plain RMS: the unweighted level difference, for reference. Older or clinical listeners and real headphones may differ. How this is computed.

Data: data.json from the export script.

Cause

getGain computes the filters' gain change for each shifted window and gainAdapt applies it at the next zero crossing, but only when bGainAdapt is 1. getAudapterDefaultParams sets gainAdapt = 0 and AudapterIO sends it.

getAudapterDefaultParams has set gainAdapt = 0 since Audapter 2.1.5 (upstream and blab alike); the C++ default is 1.

Options

Decide deliberately. p.gainAdapt = 1 equalises the unweighted level but not the heard level (with it on, lowering F1 makes the voice quieter, median -1.4 dBA here), so it does not remove the cue. Keep 0 and treat the level as part of the manipulation, logging it (A-weighted signalOut level per trial), or match the A-weighted level per condition. Either way, a check of signalOut level by condition in existing data shows the size of the cue. The gain-adaptation state (static gain, formant notes F14) did not carry over between trials in our test.

How we know

  • R reading: notes/formant.md F14: gainAdapt/gainPerturb keep static gain and lastSample across trials

  • H independent check by the coordinator (plain RMS): a_fmtlevel.m VERIFY-FMT-LEVEL: F1 −125 mel +4.9 to +7.0 dB RMS, +125 mel −1.0 to −3.8 dB RMS on three ARCTIC sentences

F6

Medium severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

An undocumented blab change that vsaSentence depends on: a field perturbation switches on again every time the formants re-enter the field (and minVowelLen has no effect)

Touches blab's current experiments: vsaSentence depends on this behaviour, and the other VSA experiments use the same restricted field. It is an undocumented behaviour change, not a defect for blab; it matters for anyone running these designs on Audapter 2.1.5 or another fork.
Relevant blab studies affected. Affected by design: vsaSentence depends on the re-arming, and vsaCentralize and vsaGeneralize use the same restricted field. The uniform whole-plane fields (attentionComp, coAdapt, uhdapter) are unaffected.

What happens

This is a question about documentation, not a defect: blab changed the rule deliberately (the "formant dropout fix", 2020), and vsaSentence's sentence design needs it, because its field excludes consonants, so with the original one-shot rule only the first vowel of each sentence would be perturbed. In perturbation-field mode, Audapter perturbs every stretch of speech whose formants fall inside the field, each time they enter it, for the whole trial. The parameter minVowelLen, which looks like it controls how long a stretch must be, has no effect and cannot even be changed.

When it matters

Affects field-mode experiments without an OST/PCF. On multi-syllable stimuli, diphthongs and glides, later syllables and returns to the target vowel are perturbed too, not only the first vowel. A brief tracker excursion out of the field does not end the perturbation. With a PCF loaded, the PCF decides per OST state and this does not apply. Across 80 real recordings this roughly doubles the perturbed frames compared with perturbing one stretch per trial.

Example

A field that raises F1 by 20 % while F1 is at least 600 Hz. On a 1 s /a/ → /i/ → /a/ glide, F1 leaves the field and comes back: Audapter shifts both /a/ stretches (0.12–0.35 s, 0.88–1.20 s), so the final /a/ is heard at 909 Hz instead of the spoken 778 Hz. A one-shot rule would shift only the first (0.12–0.35 s). On a steady /a/ with a brief F1 dip, the shift resumes after the dip.

Run it in your browser

This runs both inputs through the real Audapter C++ core compiled to WebAssembly from the pinned commit, once with the current behaviour and once with a one-shot-per-trial rule (the change below, which restores the end-of-stretch rule). The one-shot build gives bit-identical output whenever the formants never leave the field. Which rule is right depends on the experiment.

Data: data.json from the export script.

Cause

In field mode, detectTrans() decides each voiced frame whether the formants are in the field. The rule that ended the perturbation when the formants left the field after at least minVowelLen frames (setting transDone, which disables detection until the next reset()) is commented out, so transDone is never set; its else branch can no longer run, and minVowelLen is read nowhere. Separately, minvowellen is registered as an int parameter but stored in a double, so setting it writes 4 bytes into the double and the value stays at 60 frames whatever is set (our sweep: identical output for 5, 60 and 1000).

Introduced deliberately in the blab-lab fork (commit deab341, "Formant dropout fix v1", 2020), so that a brief tracker excursion out of the field no longer ends the perturbation for the rest of the trial.

Options

Choose and document one rule. If re-arming is intended, remove transDone, minVowelLen and the dead branch. If one stretch per trial is wanted, report/patches/f6-restore-transdone.patch restores it (4 lines); a parameter could offer both. Either way, store minVowelLen in a type the setter matches.

How we know

  • H report export: report_f6.m glide + dip + minVowelLen sweep; the one-shot comparison runs the same script on a 2.1.5 build
  • H first analysis (F1 850 → 400 → 850 Hz): a_reentry.m a second shifted stretch after re-entry
  • H WASM one-shot build: report/wasm/checks/alt-f6.mjs matches the one-shot comparison to the frame; bit-identical to the current build when the field is never left and on 6 reference scenarios

Also relevant to current experiments (small effects)

FMT-F3 Medium R

The 2D perturbation field uses the lower-left grid cell, not interpolation

What happens. The 2D field lookup rounds both grid positions down and ignores the fractional part, although the comments say linear interpolation. The perturbation is piecewise constant, biased by up to one grid step toward lower F1/F2, and the last row and column are never used.

When it matters. Affects 2D-field experiments whose fields change noticeably between grid points. Rows are F1 and columns F2 consistently.

Introduced in the blab-lab fork.

Fix. Interpolate bilinearly, or document the nearest-lower-cell rule.

How we know. By reading. Audit notes

CORPUS-7 Low H

With pitch shifting on, low frequencies are boosted more than the rest: +7 dB at 30 Hz

What happens. At 0 semitones the phase vocoder adds +3.5 dB above 150 Hz (PT-5) and more below: +3.6 dB at 100 Hz, +4.0 at 80, +5.7 at 50 and +7.0 dB at 30 Hz. Measured on the audio, the bus noise alone rises by +3.5 dBA (+3.3 to +3.3 phon, ISO 532-1): most of the added energy is below 100 Hz, where the ear is less sensitive, so the heard change is smaller than the unweighted level change.

When it matters. Affects pitch-shift sessions in rooms with low-frequency noise: in a recording with bus noise, the noise alone rose by +3.5 dBA and the noisy speech as a whole by +3.6 dBA: the extra low-frequency energy is large in unweighted level but adds little that the ear weights, so the balance of noise and voice at the ear barely changes. It matters more for analyses of unweighted level or of low-frequency content in the output.

Level and loudness: for vocoder off vs on, the heard level changes by +3.5 dBA and the loudness level by +3.3 to +3.3 phon (ISO 532-1, 60–85 dB SPL): at least 1 phon at every presentation level, above the ~1 dB just-noticeable difference. Level and loudness agree here: the change is close to a pure gain.

Questions for the lab, from the public experiment code

We read the lab's public experiment scripts and found three things, of different weight. One is a real open question: as committed, the public vsaGeneralize runner, which its public experiment script calls, perturbs the baseline trials and never scales the field (LAB-2); the lab's logs can settle it, and the later vsaGeneralize2 study is wired correctly. One is repository hygiene: vsaCentralize's repository ships an unused runner with wrong field wiring, while the runner its experiment calls is correct (LAB-1). One is a known, harmless dead setting: p.fb4Gain never reaches Audapter, as the lab's own code already notes, so every fb 4 study used the same default level (LAB-3). Every parameter sequence was reproduced exactly, with the lab's own calc_pertField, through Audapter. This is a reading of public code, not a claim about published results.

For reference, vsaSentence is wired as designed: it sends the mel grids after init (run_vsaSentence_audapter.m lines 67–71 @c01942f), and at strength 0.5 every vowel is heard 0.49–0.50 of the way to the centre (intended 0.50). That wiring, also used by the runner vsaCentralize's experiment calls, is the "Expected" in LAB-1 and LAB-2.

Two small script defects found by running the public code (see "Running the lab's own code"): free-speech's modelComp template calls run_checkLPC(expt, exptPre) with exptPre never defined (run_modelComp_expt.m line 33 @ec961b7), so it stops when the LPC check is chosen; and attentionAdapt's server-down branch assigns expt.session but then reads expt.sessionOrder (run_attentionAdapt_expt.m lines 126–136 @0f4ef43), so the experiment cannot start when the lab server is unreachable. Neither affects data that was collected.

LAB-1

Low severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

vsaCentralize's public repository ships an unused runner whose field wiring is wrong; the runner the experiment actually calls is wired correctly

A repository-hygiene note, not an Audapter defect and not a question about the lab's data. It matters to anyone who reuses the public runner as a template for a new vowel-space experiment.
Relevant blab studies safe as run; unused public copy mis-wired. vsaCentralize is safe as run: its experiment script calls run_vsaAdapt_audapter (in blab's unpublished code, not in the public repository), which sends the mel grids after init, as vsaSentence does. The public run_vsaAdapt2_audapter.m is called by no script, and it is mis-wired.

What the design intends

Each vowel should be heard partway toward the centre of the speaker's own vowel space. The lab's calc_pertField('in', fmtMeans, 1) builds a 257 × 257 field in mel: at every F1–F2 point the shift points toward the centroid of the speaker's corner vowels and its size is the distance to it. The experiment script scales that field by shiftScaleFact, which is 0.5 in the hold phase for the adapt group, so a vowel is heard 50 % of the way to the centre.

What the unused public runner does

Audapter looks up each frame's formants on the grid in pertf1/pertf2. calc_pertField returns mel grids in p.pertF1/p.pertF2. The runner the experiment calls re-sends those. The unused public runner instead re-sends p.pertf1/p.pertf2 (lower case) right after AudapterIO('init'): the Hz grids (200–1500 and 500–3500) the experiment script stored earlier. MATLAB field names are case-sensitive; Audapter's parameter names are not, so the Hz grid silently replaces the mel grid. The formants (in mel) are then looked up at the wrong cell of the field, and each vowel receives the shift meant for a different point of the vowel space.

Example

What someone reusing the public run_vsaAdapt2_audapter.m would get. On a real sustained /i/ (PVQD speaker LA9015), at strength 0.5: the design intends F2 to fall toward the centre; with the public runner's wiring, F2 rises. Measured on the audio: spoken F1 305 Hz, F2 2292 Hz; correctly wired F1 355 Hz, F2 1926 Hz; public runner F1 345 Hz, F2 2562 Hz. On six synthetic vowels at the lab's default means, 4 of 6 (/i/, /æ/, /ɪ/, /ɛ/) move away from the centre, and every heard vowel misses the intended one by 76–250 mel. Wired correctly (the called runner, and vsaSentence), the same field moves every vowel 0.49–0.50 of the way to the centre, as designed.

Audit notes
Findings log

An open question for vsaGeneralize: as committed, the runner its experiment script calls perturbs the baseline trials by 201–490 mel and gives the training trials the full, unscaled field; the lab's logs can settle it

A question about the lab's public experiment code, not an Audapter defect. The public experiment script calls this public runner; the version that collected the data could still differ from the committed one. This is a reading of public code, not a claim about published results; the lab's public data (OSF 78z93) can settle it.
Relevant blab studies affected. vsaGeneralize: its public experiment script calls this public runner, so this is the open question. The lab's later vsaGeneralize2 study is not affected: it sends the mel grids and scales pertAmp2D.

What the design intends

"A non-uniform auditory perturbation of vowel formants that centralizes all vowels" (README). Baseline-training trials have strength 0 (no perturbation); training trials have strength 0.5, so each vowel is heard halfway to the centre of the speaker's vowel space; generalization trials are unperturbed and masked (fb 4).

What the committed code does

calc_pertField switches on the two-dimensional field (bShift2D = 1) at full strength, and AudapterIO('init') sends it. Per trial, the committed runner scales only the one-dimensional pertAmp, which is all zeros, so the two-dimensional field is never scaled: it stays at full strength on every fb 3 trial, including strength 0. The runner also re-sends the Hz grids (as in vsaCentralize), so the full-strength field is looked up in the wrong place.

Example

On a real sustained /ɑ/ (PVQD speaker LA9015) on a baseline-training trial (strength 0): the design intends no change; as committed, F2 is raised by 761 Hz. Measured on the audio: spoken F1 673 Hz, F2 1163 Hz; intended F1 673 Hz, F2 1163 Hz; as committed F1 523 Hz, F2 1923 Hz. On six synthetic vowels every one is shifted, by 201–490 mel, and the training-phase shifts are identical to the baseline ones. Confirmed by running the committed vsaGeneralize experiment script and runner end to end for a full session (466 trials, unmodified code; see "Running the lab's own code"): baseline-training trials at strength 0 are shifted like training trials in every one of eight AI-generated voices: 0.29–0.37 s per trial, median 177–236 mel in F1 and 334–424 mel in F2, heard F2 ×1.51–1.70. The lab's logs can settle whether this runner collected the data.

How to check

In the public data (OSF 78z93): on baseline-training trials (shiftScaleFact = 0) every frame should have sfmts == fmts. Audit notes
Findings log

A dead line in the public vsaGeneralize script: p.fb4Gain = 0.98 never reaches Audapter, so the noise plays at the default level, as in every blab fb 4 study

Informational. For everyone: AudapterIO('init') silently ignores fields of p it does not know, so a misspelt or non-existent parameter has no effect and no warning; check the saved data.params for the value you meant.
Relevant blab studies safe as run. Safe as run, and already noted in the lab's own code: blab's unpublished runners (vsaGeneralize2, biteblockAdapt, trainingVarGen, sponAdapt2) carry comments that fb4Gain is not an Audapter parameter, that the real one is fb4GainDB (default 10 dB), and that none of their experiments change it. So every blab fb 4 study, vsaGeneralize included, played the noise at the same default level; only the 0.98 in the public script suggests otherwise.

What the line suggests

In the generalization phases (fb 4, speech-modulated masking noise) the script sets the noise gain to 0.98 (p.fb4Gain = 0.98), just under unity.

What the committed code does

AudapterIO('init') forwards only p.fb4GainDB, in decibels; a field called fb4Gain is ignored without a warning. Audapter therefore uses its default of 10 dB, not the −0.18 dB that 0.98 corresponds to.

Example

A real sentence (CMU ARCTIC bdl "Will we ever forget it.") in fb 4 with the bundled babble. Measured on the audio: at the gain the line suggests (0.98) the output would be -42.4 dBFS (A-weighted); at the default level that actually plays, -32.2 dBFS (10.2 dBA louder).

Trial-to-trial carry-over in mixed designs

Carrie Niziolek asked whether, in designs where perturbed trials are followed by unperturbed ones, one trial's lingering state can affect the next. As blab runs its experiments, it does not. With other OST rules or other ways of switching conditions, it can, and the effect is large and silent. This section shows both.

blab's switching methods: no carry-over

We ran each method the lab uses to change the condition between trials, with the lab's own settings and OST files, in mixed sessions of perturbed and catch trials, once in order and once in reverse order.

How the condition changes between trialsUsed byResult
Field mode: setParam pertAmp/pertPhi before each trial (0 on catch trials); OST and PCF cleared at the start attentionComp, coAdapt, uhdapter, the VSA experiments, the free-speech template Catch trials: 0.000 s shifted; F1 heard/spoken 0.998–1.009. Perturbed trials: exactly ±125 mel logged. Reversing the trial order changes nothing: 7 of 7 trials identical in the log, 8 of 8 in the audio.
PCF rewritten and reloaded before each trial, OST loaded once simonMultisyllable (seven/sever, pedigree), simonSingleWord v2 Catch trials: 0.000 s shifted. The shift ends at the detected vowel offset on every perturbed trial. 7 of 7 trials identical in either order.
AudapterIO('init', p) before each trial simonSingleWord v2; blab's pitch experiments (pitchAdaptPD, pitchComp) Re-sends every parameter, including pitchShiftRatio, so the pitch carry-over below cannot occur.

Across all 69 OST files in blab's public and unpublished experiment code, every one of the 57 INTENSITY_FALL rules comes after a rule in the same trial that refreshes the stored time, so none can read the previous trial's value (blab's timeWrap uses the RMS-floor rule for a burst onset, but a rise-and-hold rule runs before its FALL). No blab OST has a maxIOI timeout. The one remaining difference between trials is cosmetic: the first trial after MATLAB starts logs slightly different formants for its first 36 ms of voicing (the tracker's memory; the audio is identical). Evidence: exp_mixed.m (S1, S2), exp_simon_session.m; log entries EXP-2, EXP-6, EXP-10.

What to avoid: when carry-over does happen

OST-F1 · offset detected later every trial

Affected if an INTENSITY_FALL rule has no refreshing rule before it in the same trial: the only rules before it are ELAPSED_TIME, the RMS-floor rule (…_WITH_RMS_FLOOR, mode 32) or the ratio rules (INTENSITY_RATIO_RISE, INTENSITY_RATIO_FALL_HOLD). These do not refresh the stored time; every other rule does. Reloading the OST or re-running init does not help.

Safe if any rise-and-hold, slope, stretch, FALL or AND_RATIO rule runs before the FALL in the same trial, as in every blab OST.

COORD-1 · a PCF left loaded from an earlier block

Affected if a field-mode block follows any block that loaded an OST/PCF (every blab session starts with the measureFormants calibration) and does not clear them. AudapterIO('init') does not.

Safe if the runner calls Audapter('ost', '', 0); Audapter('pcf', '', 0); first, as every blab field-mode runner does.

OST-F5 · pitch catch trials shifted

Affected if pitch catch trials are made with Audapter('pcf', '', 0) after a trial that ended while shifted, without re-running init.

Safe if catch trials load an all-zero PCF, or init runs before every trial.

OST-F2 · maxIOI timeout drifts

Affected if the OST has a maxIOI (timeout) section and is loaded once for many trials.

Safe if there is no maxIOI section (all blab OSTs), or the OST is reloaded before every trial.

OST-F1

High severity

  • H Harness
  • D Driver
  • F Formal

Audit notes
Findings log

With some OST rule combinations, the "speech has ended" rule fires later on every trial, so a perturbation meant to stop at the end of a word runs on into the next word

Not triggered by any blab design we inspected: in all 69 blab OST files, public and unpublished, every INTENSITY_FALL has a rule that refreshes the stored time earlier in the same trial. Affects any design in which the only rules before an INTENSITY_FALL are ELAPSED_TIME, blab's RMS-floor onset rule (INTENSITY_RATIO_ABOVE_THRESH_WITH_RMS_FLOOR) or a ratio rule.
Relevant blab studies safe as run. Safe as run: no blab OST, public or unpublished, has an INTENSITY_FALL preceded only by ELAPSED_TIME, the RMS-floor rule or a ratio rule (timeWrap uses the RMS-floor rule for onset, followed by a rise-and-hold rule).

What happens

An OST remembers the frame at which a level-based rule last ended (lastStatEnd). INTENSITY_FALL, the usual "speech has ended" rule, may only fire once more than its minimum time has passed since that frame. Audapter('reset') does not clear the stored frame, and neither does reloading the OST or AudapterIO('init'). Rules that record their own end (the rise-and-hold, slope and stretch rules, and INTENSITY_FALL itself) overwrite it in every trial, so a FALL after them works. ELAPSED_TIME and the RMS-floor rule never write it, and the ratio rules write it only in a state that a normally numbered rule never reaches. A FALL right after one of those rules therefore waits for a frame from an earlier trial: the detected offset can never come earlier than the previous trial's offset plus the minimum time. It creeps later on every trial, and jumps after any long trial. The perturbation that should stop at the offset stays on.

When it matters

Matters when a perturbation (or the next state) is timed from a detected offset, no rule before the FALL in the trial refreshes the stored time, and the same Audapter session runs more than one trial. It does not matter whether the earlier trials were perturbed: only how long their speech lasted. The first trial after MATLAB starts is always correct, so a single-trial pilot will not show it. Safe if any INTENSITY_RISE_HOLD, INTENSITY_RISE_HOLD_POS_SLOPE, slope, stretch, FALL or INTENSITY_AND_RATIO rule runs before the FALL in the same trial (as in blab's measureFormants, bedhead, seven/sever and pedigree OSTs), or if no rule is timed from an offset.

Example

A "shift the first word" design with catch trials: two-word trials, F1 raised 125 mel from the detected onset of word 1 to its detected offset, one catch trial in four, same OST all session and the PCF reloaded before every trial, with blab's standard settings. Onset is detected with blab's RMS-floor rule. The words are a real voice (a sustained /ɑ/ then /i/ of PVQD speaker SJ7001, cut to each trial's length). Trials 1 and 2 are correct. Trial 3 is a catch trial with a long first word (1.20 s); after it, trial 4's offset is found only at 1.45 s instead of 0.53 s, so word 2 (/i/) is heard with F1 raised (+80 % instead of +1 %; F1 253 → 454 Hz). After the second long catch trial the offset is never detected again (trials 7 and 8). The same session on synthetic vowels gives the same timings within 22 ms.

Data: data.json from the export script.

Cause

OST_TAB::reset() clears lastStatEnd, but nothing calls it: Audapter::reset() only sets stat = 0, and an OST reload frees and rebuilds the rule arrays but leaves lastStatEnd alone. INTENSITY_FALL fires only when data_counter - lastStatEnd exceeds its minimum, so a value left from an earlier trial blocks it. The RMS-floor rule, unlike the rise-and-hold rules, never sets lastStatEnd.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Safe pattern and fix

Safe pattern: put INTENSITY_FALL only after a rule that records its end (INTENSITY_RISE_HOLD or INTENSITY_RISE_HOLD_POS_SLOPE, as blab's own OSTs do); if you need the RMS-floor onset, follow it with a short rise-and-hold rule before the FALL. Reloading the OST or re-running AudapterIO('init') does not help. Fix: call ostTab.reset() from Audapter::reset() (one line, report/patches/ost-f1-reset-per-trial.patch). With it, and the OST-F2 fix, every trial behaves like the first trial of a session (proven on a model of the OST code). Check past data: in ost_stat, compare the frame at which the offset state starts across trials; a creep of about the FALL minimum per trial, or a jump after a long trial, is this bug.

How we know

  • H report export (mixed session: report_ost_f1.m
  • H realistic mixed-design session: exp_mixed.m SCEN=S5 EXP-9: shift runs 0.84 s into word 2 after a long catch trial
  • H harness test: t_ost.m FAIL “OST F1: trial B (after A) offset detected”: burst ends 0.40 s, state 2 at 1.678 s
  • D standalone driver of ost.cpp: scratch/ost-pcf/t/drv.cpp fall_leak offset at frame 200 fired at frame 815
  • F Lean 4 proof: formal/lean/Ost.lean with both fixes

Reproduce cd audit/harness && ./run-oct.sh exp_mixed.m

COORD-1

Medium severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

A PCF loaded earlier in the session stays loaded through AudapterIO('init') and overrides a later field-mode experiment: shift trials are not shifted, or no-shift trials are

blab's runners are protected: every blab field-mode runner we inspected clears the OST and PCF before AudapterIO('init'). Affects any runner that leaves out those two lines, for example a copy of a runner or a new experiment run in the same MATLAB session after an OST/PCF block.
Relevant blab studies safe as run. Safe as run: every blab field-mode runner clears the OST and PCF before AudapterIO('init').

What happens

An OST or PCF stays loaded until Audapter('ost', '', 0) and Audapter('pcf', '', 0) clear it. Audapter('reset') and AudapterIO('init', p) do not. While a PCF is loaded, it decides every formant shift, and the perturbation field set with pertAmp/pertPhi is ignored. Every blab formant session starts with the measureFormants calibration block, which loads an OST and an all-zero PCF, so a field-mode experiment that follows it without clearing them delivers no shift at all.

When it matters

Matters when a field-mode block follows any block that loaded an OST/PCF in the same MATLAB session. With the calibration's all-zero PCF, the whole experiment is silently unperturbed; after a block with a nonzero PCF (for example a bedhead hold block), "noShift" trials are perturbed at that block's strength. Safe if the runner calls Audapter('ost', '', 0); Audapter('pcf', '', 0); before AudapterIO('init', p), as blab's attentionComp, coAdapt, uhdapter, VSA and template runners do. These two lines are load-bearing.

Example

The measureFormants calibration (two trials), then an attentionComp-style field experiment: 125 mel F1 shift set per trial with pertAmp/pertPhi, noShift trials interleaved, fb 3 with the bundled babble, a real sentence on every trial (CMU ARCTIC clb "I had faith in them."). With the clear lines, trial 3 is heard with F1 raised (+23 %). Without them, trial 3 is heard unchanged (-1 %) and the log shows no shifted frame (0.000 s instead of 1.174 s). A synthetic vowel gives the same result (+20 % vs +1 %).

OST-F5

Medium severity

  • H Harness
  • R Reading

Audit notes
Findings log

Pitch catch trials made by clearing the PCF can be heard at the full pitch shift, when the trial before ended while shifted

Not triggered by any blab design we inspected: blab's pitch experiments (pitchAdaptPD, pitchComp) re-run AudapterIO('init', p) before every trial, which restores the pitch setting. Affects pitch designs that make catch trials with Audapter('pcf', '', 0) and do not re-run init.
Relevant blab studies safe as run. Safe as run: blab's pitch experiments (pitchAdaptPD, pitchComp) re-run AudapterIO('init', p) before every trial.

What happens

While a PCF is loaded, Audapter writes the PCF's pitch shift for the current OST state into the user parameter pitchShiftRatio on every frame. Clearing the PCF with Audapter('pcf', '', 0) leaves the last value there, and with no PCF the phase vocoder uses pitchShiftRatio for the whole trial. If the previous trial ended in a shifted state (the participant was still voicing when the trial stopped), every following "unperturbed" trial is shifted by the full amount, and data.params.pitchShiftRatio logs the shifted value.

When it matters

Matters for pitch-perturbation designs with interleaved catch or control trials made by clearing the PCF, when a perturbed trial can end before the OST returns to an unshifted state: sustained-vowel designs, or trials cut off mid-word. If the perturbed trial ends after the shift is switched off, the catch trial is clean. Safe if catch trials load an all-zero PCF, or AudapterIO('init', p) runs before every trial (it re-sends pitchShiftRatio), or the script sets pitchShiftRatio after clearing the PCF.

Example

A sustained-vowel pitch design: +2 semitones from the detected voice onset until the level falls, phase vocoder, catch trials interleaved, on a real sustained /a/ (PVQD speaker SJ7001). The speaker is still voicing when each perturbed trial stops. With catch trials made by loading an all-zero PCF, catch trial 2 is heard at 0 cents. Made with Audapter('pcf', '', 0), it is heard at +198 cents, the whole perturbation, and data.params.pitchShiftRatio logs 1.1225. A synthetic vowel gives the same (0 cents vs +200 cents).

Cause

With a PCF loaded, each frame overwrites p.pitchShiftRatio[0] with the current state's pitch shift. After Audapter('pcf', '', 0), pertCfg.n is 0, the overwrite stops, and the vocoder keeps using the last value written. data.params reports the overwritten value.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Safe pattern and fix

Safe pattern: make catch trials by loading an all-zero PCF, or re-run AudapterIO('init', p) before every trial as blab's pitch experiments do. Fix: keep the PCF's ratio in a separate variable, so that clearing the PCF returns to the user's pitchShiftRatio. Check past data: catch trials whose data.params.pitchShiftRatio is not 1 were shifted.

OST-F2

Medium severity

  • H Harness
  • D Driver
  • F Formal

Audit notes
Findings log

After an OST maxIOI timeout, the next ELAPSED_TIME lasts one frame, and without reloading the OST the timeout fires 0.2 s later in every trial

Not triggered: no blab OST we inspected has a maxIOI (timeout) section. Affects OSTs with a timeout that are loaded once for many trials.
Relevant blab studies n.a.. Not applicable: no blab OST we inspected has a maxIOI section.

What happens

When a maxIOI rule moves the OST to a later state, Audapter records the time of that jump against the wrong state. An ELAPSED_TIME rule in the new state then fires on the next frame instead of after its duration. The wrong record also shifts the reference that later timeouts are measured from, so if the OST is not reloaded between trials, each trial's timeout fires later than the one before.

When it matters

Affects OST files with a maxIOI section, on trials where the timeout actually fires, typically quiet or unusual productions where onset detection fails. The one-frame ELAPSED_TIME happens on every such trial. The growing delay happens only when the OST is loaded once and several trials run with reset() between them; reloading the OST before each trial removes the delay but not the one-frame ELAPSED_TIME.

Example

A soft talker: a real sustained /a/ (PVQD speaker SJ7001) that never reaches the onset threshold, so the 0.2 s timeout must start the sequence, and F1 is raised 30 % from 0.1 s after the timeout. Intended: the shift starts at 0.30 s in every trial. With the OST loaded once and reset() between trials, it starts at 0.20, 0.41 and 0.61 s in trials 1–3: the ELAPSED_TIME state lasts one frame instead of 0.1 s, and every trial's timeout comes 0.2 s later than the last.

This runs one session of three trials, with the OST loaded once, through the real Audapter C++ core compiled to WebAssembly from the pinned commit: once with the current code and once with the one-line fix below.

The change in the “fix-ost-f2” build: report/patches/ost-f2-maxioi-onset-index.patch
ost.cppstatOnsetIndices[stat] = frame_counter;statOnsetIndices[j] = frame_counter;    /* audit fix OST-F2: was [stat] */

How big, how often

real voiceShift onset, trials 1 / 2 / 3 (intended 0.30 s)0.20 / 0.41 / 0.61 s
syntheticTimeout, trials 1 / 2 / 3, OST loaded once0.20 / 0.40 / 0.61 s (intended 0.20 s)

Data: data.json from the export script.

Cause

When a maxIOI rule fires, the loop that should record the onset of each state it jumps over writes statOnsetIndices[stat], the state being left, instead of statOnsetIndices[j]. ELAPSED_TIME in the new state then measures from a stale onset and fires at once. State 0's onset is overwritten with the timeout frame and never cleared, so the next trial's timeout is measured from it.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Safe pattern and fix

Write statOnsetIndices[j] in the maxIOI loop (report/patches/ost-f2-maxioi-onset-index.patch, one line). Together with the OST-F1 fix this is proven sufficient. The OST-F1 fix alone removes the growing delay but not the one-frame ELAPSED_TIME. Workaround: reload the OST before every trial, and avoid ELAPSED_TIME directly after a maxIOI target.

How we know

  • H harness test: t_ost.m FAIL “OST F2: maxIOI trial 1 ELAPSED 0.1 s in state 2”: state 2 held 0.002 s
  • H harness test: t_ost.m FAIL “OST F2: no-reload trial 2 timeout at 0.2 s”: state 2 at 0.404 s
  • H harness test: t_ost.m FAIL “OST F2: no-reload trial 3 timeout at 0.2 s”: state 2 at 0.606 s
  • H report export (vowel, audible): report_ost_f2.m vowel input, so the effect is audible
  • H WASM patch check: report/wasm/checks/fix-ost-f2.mjs fix-ost-f2 removes both symptoms; a configuration without maxIOI stays bit-identical
  • D standalone driver of ost.cpp: scratch/ost-pcf/t/drv.cpp maxioi_onset, maxioi_trials state 2 entered at frame 101, left at 102; timeouts at frames 101, 202, 303
  • F Lean 4 proof, theorem trial_independent: formal/lean/Ost.lean with both fixes, trials no longer depend on earlier trials; clearing statOnsetIndices is not needed
  • F Lean 4 counterexamples: formal/lean/OstCex.lean the reset fix alone leaves the one-frame ELAPSED_TIME; the [j] fix alone leaves OST-F1 (ce2_bug_trial1, ce2_bug_drift, ce1_leak)

Reproduce cd audit/harness && ./run-oct.sh t_ost.m

Pitfalls for future designs

None of these is triggered by the blab designs we inspected. Each can affect a plausible design, so each card states the settings that trigger it, the safe pattern, and the fix. Examples use the most plausible settings a lab would choose and are marked as hypothetical.

OST-NUM

Medium severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

An ELAPSED_TIME rule numbered as if it advanced two states runs twice, so a 100–200 ms post-onset delay becomes 200–400 ms and the shift misses a short vowel; Audapter does not check the numbering

Affects OST files where a one-state rule (ELAPSED_TIME, INTENSITY_FALL) is followed by a rule numbered two states later, an easy slip because most level rules do span two states.
Relevant blab studies n.a.. Not applicable as far as we know: blab's OST files number their rules correctly, apart from free-speech's measureFormants.ost, whose doubled INTENSITY_FALL is harmless there (EXP-2).

What happens

Each OST rule owns the states from its own number up to the next rule's number. Level rules such as INTENSITY_RISE_HOLD use two states, but ELAPSED_TIME and INTENSITY_FALL move on after one. If the next rule is numbered two higher anyway, the one-state rule is applied again in the unused state in between: its time runs twice, and any PCF rows written for "the rule's two states" apply for twice as long. Audapter accepts the file without a warning.

When it matters

Matters for timed designs: a random delay after the detected onset, a fixed perturbation duration, or a hold before the next event. Safe if every ELAPSED_TIME or INTENSITY_FALL rule is followed by a rule numbered one higher, and the PCF's shifted rows match the states the rules actually use. Checking ost_stat of a pilot trial shows the doubled states.

Example

A plausible design, not one blab runs: F1 raised 125 mel for 0.2 s, starting a random 100–200 ms after the detected voice onset, on a short real vowel (0.35 s). Numbered correctly, the shift starts 0.10 s, 0.15 s and 0.20 s after onset and covers 190, 140 and 90 ms of the vowel. With every rule numbered two apart it starts 0.20 s, 0.30 s and never after onset and covers 88, 0 and 0 ms: at the longest delay the vowel is over before the shift begins. The shift state itself lasts 0.40 s instead of 0.20 s (from ost_stat).

Cause

osTrack picks the rule whose number range contains the current state, so a rule numbered two below the next one also handles the state in between; ELAPSED_TIME then measures its duration again from that state's onset.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Safe pattern and fix

Safe pattern: number each rule by the states the previous rule uses (+1 after ELAPSED_TIME and INTENSITY_FALL, +2 after the level rules). Fix: reject or warn at load when a rule's range contains more states than its mode uses (the notes' OST F7 check).

FMT-PATCH

Medium severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

A 2-D perturbation patch built for one vowel shifts every formant outside it by the edge cell's amount, unless F1Min..F2Max are set to the patch; tokens 63 mel away get a fixed shift instead of none

Affects 2-D field designs whose grid (pertF1/pertF2) covers only part of the formant space, when F1Min..F2Max are not set to the grid.
Relevant blab studies n.a.. The public VSA studies send the field's bounds with the field (calc_pertField returns them), so they are not affected; any design that builds a small patch and leaves F1Min..F2Max at their defaults is.

What happens

Audapter looks up each frame's F1–F2 on the 2-D grid, but it clamps the lookup to the grid's edge: a formant pair outside the grid gets the shift of the nearest edge cell. Only F1Min..F1Max and F2Min..F2Max decide whether a frame is shifted at all, and they default to the whole range. A patch meant to act only around one vowel therefore also shifts transitions, other vowels and outlier tokens, each by a fixed amount taken from the patch's edge.

When it matters

Matters for per-vowel or per-token patches (for example scaling each token toward its vowel's centre, or pushing one vowel's variability in or out). Safe if F1Min..F1Max and F2Min..F2Max are sent with the patch and equal its grid limits, as calc_pertField does; then formants outside the patch are left alone.

Example

A plausible design: a ±90 mel patch around a male /ɛ/ that moves each token half-way to the vowel's centre. Tokens inside the patch are moved as designed in both runs. Two outlier tokens, 150 and 215 mel from the centre, are left alone when the patch's bounds are sent (0 and 0 mel of shift) but are shifted by 49 and 63 mel without them, the edge cell's shift.

INIT-PERSIST

Medium severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

AudapterIO('init') only sends the optional fields present in p, so a setting from an earlier block stays on: a formant block after a pitch block keeps the phase vocoder, +3.5 dBA louder

Affects sessions that run several blocks in one MATLAB session and build p for a later block without the optional fields an earlier block set (bPitchShift, rmsFF_fb, the time-domain pitch settings, fb gains).
Relevant blab studies safe as run. Safe as run, as far as we know: blab's runners build p from getAudapterDefaultParams, which always contains bPitchShift. Related to COORD-1 (a PCF that survives init).

What happens

AudapterIO('init', p) sends many parameters only if isfield(p, …). A field missing from p is not reset to a default: Audapter keeps whatever the previous block set. data.params then shows the kept value, but the script's own p does not.

When it matters

Matters when the parameter struct is built fresh for each block (for example from a saved struct or by hand) rather than from getAudapterDefaultParams. Safe if every block starts from getAudapterDefaultParams, or sets every optional field it relies on explicitly, or the MEX is cleared between blocks.

Example

A plausible session: block 1 sets p.bPitchShift = 1; block 2's p is built without that field. Audapter keeps bPitchShift = 1, so in block 2 the voice is played at +3.5 dBA instead of +0.0 dBA re the input (real sentence, measured on the audio).

WARP-48

Medium severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

At frameLen 48 (24 kHz) a time warp delivers only 73 % of the programmed lag: a 60 ms slow-down gives 44 ms

Affects time-warp (PCF warp) designs run at frameLen 48 with pvocHop 64, where the hop is not a whole multiple of the frame.
Relevant blab studies n.a.. Not applicable to public blab studies. It applies to any time-warp design at frameLen 48 with the default pvocHop 64, such as the timeAdapt settings in free-speech's public run_measureDuration_audapter.m.

What happens

A PCF warp slows the feedback down and then catches up, creating a programmed lag. At 24 kHz with frameLen 32 the delivered lag matches the programme; at frameLen 48 it is about three quarters of it, the ratio of frameLen to pvocHop (48 / 64). Nothing reports the difference.

When it matters

Matters whenever the size of the timing perturbation is the independent variable. Safe if frameLen divides pvocHop (for example frameLen 32 with pvocHop 64), or the delivered lag is measured and reported instead of the programmed one.

Example

A warp that slows to ×0.5 for 0.12 s (programmed lag 60 ms), held for 0.3 s, measured with a frequency sweep through Audapter: the delivered lag during the hold is 58.5 ms at frameLen 32 (97 %) and 44.0 ms at frameLen 48 (73 %).

How big, how often

sweepDelivered lag during the hold, programmed 60 ms: frameLen 32 / 4858.5 / 44.0 ms

Data: data.json from the export script.

Cause

The warp converts the programmed time into vocoder hops (pvocHop samples), but the cache it indexes advances once per processing frame. When pvocHop is not a whole multiple of frameLen the two units differ, and the lag comes out scaled by frameLen/pvocHop. The same frame/hop mismatch is the most likely cause of PT-5's gain of 2 (+6 dB) at frameLen 48 (not isolated in the code).

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Safe pattern and fix

Safe pattern: use a frameLen that divides pvocHop (32 at 24 kHz), or measure the delivered lag. Fix: convert the warp time with the same unit the cache index uses.

How we know

  • H report export (sweep: report_pitfalls2.m SCEN=warp48

TDS-ONSET

Low severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

A time-domain pitch-shift schedule counts from the first frame above the level threshold, 56–111 ms after the acoustic onset on real speech, so analyses aligned to acoustic onset misplace the perturbation

Affects time-domain (bTimeDomainShift) pitch designs with a timed schedule, especially with soft or breathy onsets.
Relevant blab studies safe as run. blab's time-domain pitch studies use perturbations that do not depend on a precise onset time as far as we know; named public studies do not use the time-domain shifter.

What happens

The schedule's clock starts when the frame level first exceeds rmsThresh, not at the acoustic onset, and it then runs only on frames above the threshold (PT-3). A step scheduled "0.2 s after onset" therefore comes 0.2 s after the level crossing, which lags the acoustic onset by an amount that depends on how soft the onset is.

When it matters

Matters for analyses that align responses to the acoustic onset, and for designs comparing speakers or conditions with different onset softness. Safe if responses are aligned to the logged perturbation time (from the output or the first above-threshold frame), not to the acoustic onset.

Example

Four ARCTIC sentences and two PVQD vowels with a soft onset, a +2 st step scheduled at 0.2 s (frameLen 64, nDelay 7): the first above-threshold frame comes 56–111 ms after the acoustic onset (level within 40 dB of the clip's peak), so the step is heard that much later than 0.2 s after the acoustic onset.

PVOC-NOISE

Low severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

At 24 kHz with frameLen 48, a phase-vocoder pitch shift lowers the level of a fricative far more than that of voiced speech (-9 to -17 dBA on a real /ʃ/, -2 to -8 dBA on the vowel after it), so a loudness cue tracks the perturbation

Affects phase-vocoder pitch shifts applied across fricatives or other noise-like segments (whole-utterance shifts, or states that include consonants).
Relevant blab studies n.a.. Not applicable to the public blab studies, which do not shift pitch.

What happens

The phase vocoder is not level-preserving (PT-5): at 0 st it raises the level, and any nonzero shift removes some of that, by an amount that depends on the signal. With frameLen 32 or 64 every segment we tried (vowel, /ʃ/, noise band) comes out 3.4 to 7.2 dBA below its 0 st level. With frameLen 48 fricatives and noise lose more, 6 to 16 dBA, and the loss does not grow steadily with the shift (−2 st loses more than −4 st).

When it matters

Matters when the perturbation covers consonants, or when the level of the feedback is analysed or should not cue the condition. Safe if the shift is confined to voiced segments (an OST state per vowel), or the level of shifted fricatives is checked and compensated.

Example

At 24 kHz, frameLen 48, for shifts of ±2 and ±4 semitones, relative to the same segment at 0 st: the real /ʃ/ of an ARCTIC sentence changes by -17.2 to -8.6 dBA in level (−4 st: -10.3 dBA); a /s/-like noise band by -14.8 to -6.4 dBA (−4 st: -6.4 dBA); the voiced stretch that follows the /ʃ/ by -7.8 to -2.0 dBA (−4 st: -7.8 dBA).

CORPUS-8

Medium severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

With the default frame settings, the logged pitch is wrong for voices below about 140 Hz

Not triggered by any blab design we inspected: none uses time-domain pitch shifting, the only mode that logs pitch. Affects time-domain pitch experiments with low voices at the default frame settings.
Relevant blab studies safe as run. Safe as run: the time-domain pitch studies (pitchAdapt, pitchComp, pitchAdaptPD) use frameLen 64 / nDelay 7 with pitch bounds set around each participant's calibrated F0.

What happens

With the time-domain pitch shifter on, Audapter tracks F0 and logs it as pitchHz. Its analysis window is frameLen × nDelay samples, 10 ms with the defaults, which holds too few cycles of a low voice. Below about 140 Hz the tracker returns a higher, wrong value, and the shifter's F0 filter is centred on it.

When it matters

Affects time-domain pitch shifting with the default frameLen 32 / nDelay 5 for typical adult male voices (85–130 Hz) and some low female voices. pitchHz and shiftedPitchHz are then not F0. The heard shift stayed close to target on real speech. With frameLen 64 / nDelay 7 (28 ms), as in Audapter's own time-domain shift demo, it is correct.

Example

Cause

The tracker picks the strongest cepstral peak between the pitch bounds, but the cepstrum comes from the formant tracker's analysis buffer. A pitch period longer than about half the window gives no cepstral peak, so the search returns a spurious one.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Safe pattern and fix

Warn when 2 / pitchLowerBoundHz is longer than the analysis window, or size the pitch analysis from the pitch bounds. Workaround: use frameLen 64 / nDelay 7 for low voices.

How we know

CORPUS-10

Medium severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

After a change of frameLen or nDelay in the same session, runFrame can hang forever at 100 % CPU

Not triggered by blab's runners: they change frameLen only together with the sample rate, followed by AudapterIO('init'), which rebuilds the tracker. Affects designs that change frameLen or nDelay at a fixed sample rate in one MATLAB session.
Relevant blab studies safe as run. Safe as run: blab runners change frameLen only together with the sample rate, followed by AudapterIO('init').

What happens

Changing frameLen, nDelay or nWin does not rebuild the formant tracker. The stale tracker can produce NaN LPC coefficients, and the root finder then loops forever because it has no iteration limit. In an experiment this freezes the audio callback and MATLAB.

When it matters

Needs a frame-setting change within one MATLAB session, for example switching between a formant and a time-domain pitch condition with different frame settings. It depends on the audio: of four real clips run through the same switch, one hung. A fresh session with the same settings is fine.

Example

A sung phrase (vocadito_4) with the time-domain pitch shifter, one trial at frameLen 32 / nDelay 5, then AudapterIO('init') with frameLen 64 / nDelay 7 and the same clip again. The second trial's first runFrame call never returns: no frame completes in 62 s at 99–100 % CPU. In a fresh session the same trial processes all 1150 frames in 0.12 s.

Build
blab-lab audapter_mex as shipped (@169cadf)
All settings: parameters, OST and PCF, each line explained

No recordings: nothing comes out while the process is hung.

How big, how often

real speechFrames completed: fresh session / after the switch1150 / 0
real speechCPU while hung99.4–100.2 %
real speechTime until killed62 s (240 s in an independent re-run)
real speechClips that hang after the same switch1 of 4

Data: data.json from the export script.

Cause

hqr_roots uses the QR iteration from Numerical Recipes without its limit of 30 iterations, so NaN coefficients make it loop forever. The NaNs come from the formant tracker, which framelen, ndelay and nwin do not mark for rebuilding (I-09).

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Safe pattern and fix

Cap the iterations and skip the frame, check the LPC coefficients with isfinite, and rebuild the tracker when frame settings change. Workaround: after changing frameLen, nDelay or nWin, change nLPC or bCepsLift in a throw-away AudapterIO('init') and restore it, or clear Audapter.

How we know

  • H hang reproduction on real speech: harness/oct/corpus_tdshang.m SCEN=vocadito_4 VARIANT=after32
  • H report export with timing and CPU samples: harness/oct/report_corpus10.sh kills the container after a set time without progress; the fresh-session control completes

Reproduce cd audit/harness && oct/report_corpus10.sh 60

LIVE-1 / LIVE-2

Medium severity

  • D Driver

Audit notes
Findings log

Reloading OST/PCF files or rebuilding DSP objects while audio runs can crash MATLAB

Not triggered by blab's runners: every one stops audio before loading files or changing parameters (stop, load, reset, start), which we found race-free. Affects always-on designs that change settings while audio runs.
Relevant blab studies safe as run. Safe as run: no blab runner keeps audio running across trials; files and parameters are changed while audio is stopped.

What happens

In always-on designs the audio keeps running while MATLAB loads a new OST or PCF, or sets parameters that rebuild the pitch shifter, phase vocoder or formant tracker. These operations free and reallocate memory that the audio callback is using at the same moment. The callback then reads a NULL pointer, which crashes MATLAB, or freed memory, which may play garbage or crash later.

When it matters

Affects designs that change OST, PCF, pitchShiftRatio with the time-domain shifter, fn1/fn2, or pvocFrameLen while audio is running, which AudapterIO('init') does in an always-on loop. Stopping audio before these calls avoids it. The usual per-trial start–stop flow is not affected. These numbers come from a simulation of the live path (the real audio code, built with GCC on Linux, with a modelled ASIO driver), so rates are indicative.

Example

A simulated always-on session reloading the PCF every 20 or 250 ms while a vowel plays: 10 crashes in 6605 reloads. Reloading the OST: 13 crashes in 3022 reloads. Each run died after between 1 and 1842 reloads.

Settings used

All settings: parameters, OST and PCF, each line explained

No recordings: the effect is a crashed process or a read of freed memory.

How big, how often

live simulationPCF reloads until a crash10 crashes in 6605 reloads (about 1 in 660)
live simulationOST reloads until a crash13 crashes in 3022 reloads (about 1 in 232)
live simulationParameter changes read after free (AddressSanitizer)pitchShiftRatio, fn1, pvocFrameLen, PCF reload with the phase vocoder

Data: data.json from the export script.

Cause

Nothing serialises the MATLAB thread and the audio callback. Reading a PCF frees the per-state arrays and sets them to NULL before allocating new ones, while pertCfg.n keeps the old count; the OST reader does the same with stat0. Several parameter setters delete and rebuild DSP objects that the callback may be using.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Safe pattern and fix

Refuse ost, pcf and object-rebuilding parameter changes while audio runs, or build into temporaries and swap them in under a lock the callback also takes. Workaround: stop audio before loading files or changing these parameters.

How we know

  • D live simulation driver, plain -O2 build: live/run.sh crash results/crash.txt plus the earlier run kept in live/work/out/crash_*.txt, pooled
  • D live simulation driver, ASan build: live/run.sh uaf heap-use-after-free for pitchshiftratio, fn1, pvocFrameLen and PCF reload with pvoc
  • D ThreadSanitizer inventory: live/run.sh tsan SEGV at ost.cpp:361 during OST reload; 195 distinct racing site pairs
  • D report export (crash counts, sanitizer lines): report/live/export_live.py live12

Reproduce audit/live/run.sh crash uaf tsan && python3 audit/report/live/export_live.py live12

LIVE-3

Medium severity

  • D Driver

Audit notes
Findings log

reset() while the participant is speaking can send a loud, clipped click to the headphones

Not triggered by blab's per-trial flow, which calls reset() while audio is stopped. Affects designs that call reset() with audio running while the participant may be speaking.
Relevant blab studies safe as run. Safe as run: no blab runner keeps audio running across trials, so reset() is never called during speech.

What happens

Audapter('reset') runs on the MATLAB thread while the audio callback may be filtering a frame. It clears the resampling filters' state in the middle of that frame, and the filter can then ring for a few milliseconds far above the speech level. The output is clipped at the sound card, so the participant hears a click.

When it matters

Affects designs that keep audio running across trials and call reset while the participant may be voicing, such as always-on designs that reset at each trial start. It happens on roughly 1 in 1000–2000 resets during voicing. The size varies from run to run; the observed range is +17 to +61 dB above the loudest normal output sample. The usual start–stop–reset flow per trial is not affected. These numbers come from a simulation of the live path (the real audio code, built with GCC on Linux, with a modelled ASIO driver), so rates are indicative.

Example

A looped vowel with reset called about every 62 ms for 120 s: 1945 resets, 1014 of them during voicing. One produced a burst of +17.0 dB above the normal peak, 6.5 ms long, with 21 samples beyond full scale. Every other reset during voicing produced only a 6 ms dropout.

How big, how often

live simulationResets during voicing / bursts, this run1014 / 1

Cause

Nothing serialises reset() with the audio callback. reset() zeroes the 48 ↔ 16 kHz resampling filters' delay lines while the callback may be inside IIR_Filter::filter; the remaining state no longer cancels and the high-order filter rings.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Safe pattern and fix

Put one lock around every MEX action that changes Audapter state; the callback tries the lock and outputs silence if it is busy. Or have reset set a flag that the callback acts on at the next frame. Workaround: stop audio before reset, or reset only while the participant is silent.

How we know

LIVE-6

Medium severity

  • D Driver

Audit notes
Findings log

If the sound card's buffer is not exactly frameLen × downFact samples, the participant hears their raw voice an octave up, chopped

Could affect any rig, including blab's: it happens whenever the sound card's buffer size differs from frameLen × downFact (96 samples at blab's settings). blab's Audapter README warns that newer Focusrite drivers crash MATLAB; whether that is related is untested.
Relevant blab studies n.a.. Depends on the rig, not the study: any study whose sound-card buffer differs from 96 samples at blab's settings.

What happens

Audapter needs audio buffers of exactly frameLen × downFact samples (96 by default). If the sound card delivers another size, Audapter silently skips processing, and the headphones get an uninitialised copy of the microphone signal read at the wrong rate: the raw voice an octave up, silent in half of every buffer.

When it matters

Affects rigs whose ASIO driver does not grant the requested buffer size; RtAudio then takes the driver's preferred size without telling Audapter. Nothing warns, and getData returns almost nothing. With a matching buffer size everything is normal. These numbers come from a simulation of the live path (the real audio code, built with GCC on Linux, with a modelled ASIO driver), so rates are indicative.

Example

A 128-sample device buffer instead of 96: over 752 callbacks, Audapter processed nothing, getData returned 1 row, and the participant heard the unprocessed voice decimated by 2 and gated on and off 375 times a second, -2.3 dBA relative to the microphone.
