CORPUS-11

Medium severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

Shifted formant targets have no upper bound, so a unit mix-up produces targets far above Nyquist and loud, clipped output

Not triggered by current blab designs, which set bRatioShift 0 and bMelShift 1 explicitly for 125 mel shifts. Affects replays of old parameter files under today's defaults, where bRatioShift is 1.
Relevant blab studies n.a.. Not applicable: current blab designs set bRatioShift 0 and bMelShift 1 explicitly.

What happens

Audapter does not limit a shifted formant to the range a filter can represent. If the perturbation amplitude is given in the wrong units, for example mel values read as ratios, the target can be tens of kilohertz and the output becomes loud and distorted.

When it matters

Happens when an old parameter set in mel units (with no bRatioShift field) is merged into today's defaults, which are ratio shift, or with any mistaken pertAmp. The C++ defaults (absolute, mel) and the MATLAB defaults (ratio) differ, which makes this easy. The logged sfmts show the absurd targets afterwards.

Example

Audapter's own 2008 example trial diao1_female, replayed with its saved parameters (mel-unit pertAmp up to 164) merged into today's defaults. In mel mode, as in 2008, F1 is raised ×1.214. Under today's ratio default F1 is multiplied by 102.8, targets reach 129992 Hz with a 6000 Hz Nyquist frequency, and the output is +13.3 dBA louder than the input, peaking at 4.6 times full scale.

Audit notes
Findings log

Reprocessing one recording under two conditions applies the second condition to the first condition's output

Not triggered by blab's offline helpers (audapter_viewer, check_audapterLPC), which build fresh frames for every run. Affects offline reprocessing that reuses one frame array for several conditions.
Relevant blab studies safe as run. Safe as run: blab's offline helpers (audapter_viewer, check_audapterLPC) build fresh frames for every run.

What happens

Audapter('runFrame', x) writes its output back into the array it is given. A script that runs the same stored frames through Audapter twice, for two conditions, feeds the first condition's output into the second.

When it matters

Affects offline reprocessing that reuses the same MATLAB variables, for example the cell array of frames in test_audapter.m, and anything else sharing that data. Scripts that build fresh frames for each run are unaffected. Live experiments are unaffected.

Example

One stored /a/ (F1 735 Hz) processed as condition 1 (F1 +20 %) and then condition 2 (F1 −20 %) from the same cell array. Condition 2 is heard at 715 Hz instead of 599 Hz, because it lowered F1 of an already raised vowel. Its logged input starts with 128 zero samples, the first condition's output delay.

I-02

Low severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

In feedback mode 5, the speech-modulated noise is scaled by dScale twice, so the noise mix changes with the rig's calibration

Not triggered: no blab experiment we inspected uses fb 5, which was added to blab in August 2026. Affects any fb 5 design with dScale other than 1.
Relevant blab studies affected. Affected: sponAdapt3 uses fb 5 (the only blab study that does, apart from a demo); its speech-to-noise balance depends on dScale.

What happens

Feedback mode 5 plays a constant noise plus a noise that follows the speaker's loudness. The speech-modulated part is multiplied by dScale twice and the constant part once, so their balance moves by 20·log10(dScale) dB instead of staying at fb5GainDB_speech.

When it matters

Affects fb 5 only. dScale comes from closedLoopGain and the lab's calibration, so two setups, or one setup at two gains, get different mixes from the same parameter. A different microphone sensitivity is compensated by the input level, so the error follows closedLoopGain. fb 4 multiplies by dScale twice as well, but has only one component, so it is a level offset there. The logged fb5GainDB_speech is the nominal value.

Example

fb 5 with babble noise and fb5GainDB_speech +20 dB. At closedLoopGain 15 dB (dScale 0.795) the speech-modulated part sits -0.7 dB relative to the constant part; at 21 dB (dScale 1.587) it sits +5.3 dB. The 6 dB gain step raises the constant noise by 6 dB and the speech-modulated noise by 12 dB.

I-03

Low severity

  • H Harness
  • F Formal

Audit notes
Findings log

A trial longer than 30 s loses its beginning, and the OST, trialLen mute and onset ramp restart at 30 s

Not triggered: blab's longest recorded trials are 4.5 s (vsaSentence). Affects trials longer than 30 s, for example sustained phonation or passage reading with an OST.
Relevant blab studies n.a.. Not applicable: blab's longest recorded trials are 4.5 s (vsaSentence).

What happens

Audapter's recorders hold 30 s at 16 kHz. When they are full, Audapter silently restarts its frame and data counters and keeps recording over the start. getData then returns only the part since the restart, and everything driven by those counters starts again: OST timing, the trialLen mute and the onset ramp.

When it matters

Affects any trial longer than 30 s, such as reading passages, continuous speech or long always-on blocks. Time-based OST rules after the restart may never fire. Shorter trials are unaffected.

Example

A 35 s trial with a vowel every second, an OST that should enter state 2 at 32 s, trialLen 34 s and a 50 ms ramp. getData returns 5.0 s (2500 rows), starting at 30 s. State 2 never comes. At 30 s the onset ramp restarts mid-vowel (-5.2 dB), and nothing is muted after 34 s.

Settings used

synthetic vowels over 35 s
Between trials
one 35 s trial
Build
blab-lab audapter_mex as shipped (@169cadf)
All settings: parameters, OST and PCF, each line explained

p.rmsThresh0.005
p.trialLen34
p.rampLen0.05

Download settings (JSON) · Open these settings in the Playground · Not replayable as a test case: needs a 35 s trial; use the full-size build with your own long recording.

Listen

  • Observed. Heard, 27-35 s of the trial (trialLen 34 s, rampLen 0.05 s) 8.0 s

    ! At 30.00 s the onset ramp restarts (a 50 ms fade-in mid-vowel), and the output is not muted at 34 s.

    No playhead: this clip is not drawn in the figure.

Heard output from 27 to 35 s: the fade-in at 30 s and the missing mute at 34 s. Synthetic only: the finding is about a 35 s recording, longer than any clip in the open corpus.

How big, how often

syntheticRecorder size / wrap time480000 samples / 30 s at 16000 Hz
syntheticReturned by getData after a 35 s trial5.0 s
syntheticState 2 (due at 32 s)never reached
syntheticOnset ramp at 30 s / mute after trialLen-5.2 dB / not muted

Data: data.json from the export script.

Cause

After each frame, handleBuffer checks whether the recorder is full and, if so, sets frame_counter and data_counter to 0. getSignal and getData return only the first frame_counter frames, and the OST, mute and ramps read the same counters.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5; the recorder grew from 14.4 s to 30 s in the blab-lab fork (commit 3c90a3a).

Safe pattern and fix

Stop recording at the end of the buffer but keep a separate trial clock, and report an overflow through getData. At minimum, have AudapterIO('getData') warn when the returned length is shorter than the time since reset. Workaround: keep trials under 30 s.

How we know

  • H sanitizer scenario (35.2 s trial): t_mem.m SCEN=long input 35.2 s, getData returned 5.20 s
  • H interface check: scratch/interface/t_wrap.m after 31 s of input, signalIn has 16000 samples (1.0 s)
  • H report export (OST, trialLen, heard output): report_i03.m 35 s trial with OST, trialLen and ramps
  • F CBMC on the verbatim recorder index code: formal/cbmc/ring.c the related recorder overrun (I-12): the write overflows exactly when frameLen does not divide 480000 and a trial reaches about 30 s; of common sizes only frameLen 512 is affected (others: 9, 18, 36, 45, 72, 90, 144, 180, …); 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 120, 128, 160, 192, 256 are safe (FORMAL-5)

Reproduce cd audit/harness && ./run-oct.sh report_i03.m

OST-F8

Low severity

  • H Harness
  • D Driver

Audit notes
Findings log

Written the way the manual describes, the INTENSITY_AND_RATIO OST rules have no hold time

Not triggered: no blab OST we inspected uses the AND_RATIO rules. Affects OSTs written with the manual's {} placeholder in field 5.
Relevant blab studies n.a.. Not applicable: no blab OST we inspected uses the AND_RATIO rules.

What happens

The INTENSITY_AND_RATIO_ABOVE_THRESH and _BELOW_THRESH rules (modes 40 and 45) read their hold time from the fifth field of the OST line, where the file format puts {}. {} reads as 0, so the rule fires on the second qualifying frame, without the intended debounce.

When it matters

Affects OST files that use modes 40 or 45 with {} in field 5, as the manual's format suggests. With a number in field 5 the hold works. How much the missing hold matters depends on the thresholds and the speaker: with the thresholds used here, the rule fired early on a synthetic fricative, but on real /sh/ onsets it fired in only 2 of 4 sentences and the held version in none, so a lab's own thresholds decide the effect.

Example

OST 0 INTENSITY_AND_RATIO_ABOVE_THRESH 0.01 1.5 <field 5> on a synthetic "sa", with +10 dB in state 2. With field 5 = 0.05 the rule holds 25 frames and state 2 starts at 0.486 s; with {} it holds 1 frame and starts at 0.438 s. A 20 ms click before the word triggers state 2 at 0.116 s with {}; with the hold, the click is ignored.

Run it in your browser

How big, how often

syntheticState 2 onset: field 5 = 0.05 / {}0.486 / 0.438 s

real speechSentences starting with /sh/ where the rule fired: hold / {}0 of 4 / 2 of 4

Data: data.json from the export script.

Cause

Modes 40 and 45 take their hold from field 5. To allow that, the parser no longer checks that field 5 is {}, and atof("{}") returns 0. The verbose printout does not show the value.

Introduced in the blab-lab fork with modes 40 and 45 (commit 9039c07).

Safe pattern and fix

Give modes 40 and 45 an explicit parameter layout: reject a non-numeric field 5 for them at load, keep the {} check for other modes, document the hold, and print it in the verbose summary. Workaround: put the hold time in field 5.

How we know

  • H harness test: t_ost.m FAIL “OST F8: AND_RATIO field-4 hold (50 ms) honoured”: onset 0.200; with {}: 0.226 s, with field5=0.05: 0.274 s
  • H report export (fricative + click, audible): report_ost_f8.m modes 40 and 45 exist only in this version
  • D standalone driver of ost.cpp: scratch/ost-pcf/t/drv.cpp hold field 5 = 0.05: 25 frames; {}: 1 frame

Reproduce cd audit/harness && ./run-oct.sh report_ost_f8.m

Further pitfalls

PT-2 / I-15 Medium H

The RMS-clip loudness protection mutes a stale 2 ms slot instead of the loud frame

What happens. When the frame RMS exceeds rmsClipThresh, the code zeroes the start of the circular output buffer instead of the current frame, so loud output passes through unchanged.

When it matters. Matters only for experiments that rely on bRMSClip for participant safety. It is off by default on the MATLAB side, and the MATLAB setters for it are commented out, so data.params reports the C++ default (on), not what the experiment script asked for.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Zero the frame at outFrameBuf_circPtr, and restore the MATLAB setters. Do not rely on this protection until then.

How we know. Harness (scratch/pitch-time/rmsclip.m): threshold 0.01, a 0.5-amplitude sine; output unchanged. Audit notes

PT-3 Medium H

The time-domain pitch-shift schedule runs on voiced time only, so shift onsets come later after every pause

What happens. The time-domain shifter's schedule clock advances only on frames above the RMS threshold. A schedule written in trial time runs late by the total time spent below threshold, and frames below threshold pass through unshifted.

When it matters. Affects time-domain pitch shifting with a time-varying schedule on speech with pauses. A 168 ms dip below threshold moved a 1.04 s onset to 1.20 s.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Advance the schedule clock on every frame, or document that the schedule is in voiced time.

How we know. Harness (scratch/pitch-time/tdsched.m). Audit notes

PT-4 Medium H

The logged pitchShiftRatio is wrong whenever the time-domain shifter is used

What happens. The pitchShiftRatio data column logs p.pitchShiftRatio[0], which the time-domain shifter does not use; it follows its own schedule. During a +100 cent time-domain shift the log says 1.0.

When it matters. Affects every analysis that reads the logged ratio from time-domain pitch-shift sessions. With a PCF loaded, the PCF's pitch values are logged although the shifter ignores them.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Log the ratio the shifter actually applies.

How we know. Harness: the logged column during a scheduled +100 cent shift. Audit notes

PT-6 Medium R

A PCF with both a pitch shift and a time warp silently drops the warp

What happens. When a PCF specifies both a pitch shift and a time warp, the phase vocoder is set to pitch-shift-only: the mode that combines both cannot be reached, because its condition repeats another branch's.

When it matters. Affects PCFs that combine pitch shift and time warp. The warp is not applied and nothing warns.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Change the third condition to warp > 0 && bIsPitchShift.

How we know. By reading. Audit notes

FMT-F4 Medium R

Clamped formants are logged during silence, where no filtering happened

What happens. The clamp branch turns the perturbation on without checking that the frame is voiced. The logged sfmts show clamp targets in silent and unvoiced frames where the formant filter did not run, and the clamp trajectory advances through silence.

When it matters. Affects clamped-formant experiments; analyses that read sfmts as "what was applied" count silent frames.

Introduced in the blab-lab fork.

Fix. Check above_rms in the clamp branch, and advance the trajectory only on voiced frames if that is the intent.

How we know. By reading. Audit notes

I-09 Medium R

Changing ndelay, frameLen or nWin does not rebuild the formant tracker

What happens. These setters do not mark the formant tracker for rebuilding, so it keeps its old analysis window.

When it matters. AudapterIO('init') usually also changes fn1/fn2, which triggers a rebuild, but a direct Audapter(3, 'ndelay', …) leaves a stale window, and in one real case a stale tracker caused a hang (CORPUS-10).

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Set bRemakeFmtTracker in these setters.

How we know. By reading; see CORPUS-10 for a consequence. Audit notes

CORPUS-3 Medium H

There is no preset for young children: the female preset underestimates their F2 by about 12 %

What happens. For 6–7-year-old children the female preset (nLPC 15) tracks F2 11.9 % low on average, with gross errors on 18 % of frames. With nLPC 11 the error is 1.7–2.0 %.

When it matters. Affects formant experiments with young children (F0 above about 220 Hz); a field or shift indexed by F2 is applied at the wrong place in the vowel space. Children aged 10–12 are tracked well with the female preset.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Add a child preset with nLPC 11, or document the choice. Workaround: set nLPC to 11 for young children.

How we know. Harness on 8 real child recordings (harness/oct/corpus_track.m, nLPC sweep); reference = frames where Praat and an independent LPC agree. Audit notes

LIVE-4 Medium D

Audapter('start') reports success when the sound card failed to open

What happens. Audapter('start') ignores the return value of the device open and marks audio as started. With a device that cannot run at 48 kHz, start returns normally, no audio flows, and getData returns a 1 × 1 result.

When it matters. Affects rigs where the driver rejects the sample rate, buffer or format. The error text goes to stdout, which on Windows is not the MATLAB command window. The playback and tone actions behave the same.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Return the open result and raise a MATLAB error on failure.

How we know. Live simulation (live/run.sh startfail): a driver without 48 kHz; start OK, 0 callbacks, getData 1 × 1. Live-path simulation: the real audioIO/RtAudio ASIO code built with GCC on Linux and driven by a fake ASIO driver; rates are indicative, not Windows-exact. Audit notes

LIVE-5 Medium D

With no ASIO driver installed, the first Audapter call of any kind crashes, even for offline processing

What happens. The audio object inside the MEX is built on the first call of any action. When no audio device exists, its constructor catches the error and then calls a method on a NULL pointer.

When it matters. Affects analysis machines without an audio interface: offline reprocessing with runFrame crashes MATLAB at the first AudapterIO('init').

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Create the audio object only when an audio action needs it, and check for NULL.

How we know. Live simulation, AddressSanitizer build (live/run.sh noasio): SEGV in RtAudio::getDeviceCount() called from audioIO.cpp:27. Live-path simulation: the real audioIO/RtAudio ASIO code built with GCC on Linux and driven by a fake ASIO driver; rates are indicative, not Windows-exact. Audit notes

PB-DSCALE Low H R

playWave plays a stored recording without dScale, so a participant hears it about 2 dBA louder than their own live feedback (a pure gain)

What happens. Live feedback is multiplied by dScale (from the closed-loop-gain calibration) before it reaches the headphones, but Audapter('playWave') sends datapb unscaled. A participant's own recording played back therefore differs in level from what they heard while speaking by −20·log10(dScale): +2.0 dB with the bundled calibration.

When it matters. Matters for speak-versus-listen designs (speech-induced suppression, where listening trials replay the speaking trials) and any comparison of self-produced feedback with played-back speech. Safe if the recording is multiplied by dScale before it is loaded as datapb.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Scale datapb by dScale before playWave, or apply dScale in the playback path.

How we know. Harness (report_pitfalls2.m SCEN=pbdscale): with the bundled calibration (dScale 0.7953) the live feedback of a real sentence leaves the device at −1.99 dB re the microphone signal; playWave sends the stored samples unscaled, so playback is +1.99 dB relative to live feedback. The playback path itself runs only on the live audio path, so that half is by reading. Audit notes

REINIT-PARAMS Low H

Re-initialising Audapter from saved data.params fails, or, once the names are fixed up, silently drops the time-domain pitch settings

What happens. data.params is Audapter's own parameter dump: it uses Audapter's names, logs rmsFF_fb empty, and leaves out the time-domain pitch settings. Feeding it back into AudapterIO('init') either fails or, after the names are mapped, rebuilds a different configuration without warning.

When it matters. Matters for offline re-analysis or OST re-tuning tools that replay trials with the saved parameters. Safe if the re-analysis starts from the experiment's own parameter struct (for example expt.audapterParams) rather than data.params.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Save the struct passed to AudapterIO with the data, or make getData log MATLAB-style names and every parameter.

How we know. Harness (report_pitfalls2.m SCEN=reinit): AudapterIO('init', data.params) stops with "structure has no member 'dScale'"; after mapping the renamed fields and refilling the empty rmsFF_fb (as a re-analysis tool must), init succeeds but bTimeDomainShift and the pitch bounds go to 0, because data.params does not contain them: a +2 st time-domain shift becomes 0 cents. Audit notes

COORD-10 Low H

A zero-length time-warp row anchored on a state that begins in the first ~0.1 s can abort the trial ("predicting the future is impossible")

What happens. A zero-length warp row (dur1 = 0), used for control trials so that every trial keeps a warp section, computes a warp offset that should be exactly 0; floating-point round-off sometimes makes it 1 ulp positive, and Audapter aborts the trial with "Error occurred during phase-vocoder time warping: predicting the future is impossible". Whether it happens depends on the exact frame at which the anchor state begins.

When it matters. Only when the anchor state begins within about the first 0.1–0.12 s of the trial; designs anchored on a detected vowel onset essentially never hit it. On the live audio path the error would be raised in the audio callback (untested; possibly a crash).

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Clamp the warp offset to ≤ 0, or compare it with a small tolerance, before the check.

How we know. Harness (report_pitfalls2.m SCEN=warpabort; 24 kHz, frameLen 32, nDelay 3; warp row anchored on state 1, tBegin 0.05, rate 0.5, dur1 0, hold 0.2): with state 1 entered at frame 26, 27, 29, 30, 34, 37 (and 20, 40) the trial aborts; at 21-25, 28, 31-33, 35, 36, 38, 39 it runs, matching the coordinator's C++ replica of the arithmetic (COORD-10). Audit notes

CORPUS-4 Low H

The male preset can report F3 as F2 for a whole vowel

What happens. On a sustained /a/ with F2 near 1000 Hz, the male preset (nLPC 17) logged F2 at 2494 Hz on every frame; nLPC 15 tracked it correctly.

When it matters. Seen on 1 of 4 male /a/ tokens. Any F2-indexed field or F2 shift is then computed from F3.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Check tracked formants against the expected vowel space during setup. Workaround: try nLPC 15 for male speakers with low F2.

How we know. Harness on real speech (harness/oct/corpus_track.m). Audit notes

LIVE-7 Low D

Missed audio callbacks are not detected: the recording is spliced silently and the logged time axis falls behind

What happens. Audapter logs each callback as the next frame, with no timestamp or overrun counter. When the driver drops periods, signalIn is spliced without a marker and the logged time, OST onsets and perturbation onsets run behind wall-clock time.

When it matters. Matters on overloaded machines or drivers without real-time priority. In the simulation, with a normal-priority driver thread on a busy CPU, 109 of 5152 periods were lost and the time axis ended 218 ms behind; with a real-time driver thread none were lost.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Count overruns from the stream time and log them per frame. Workaround: run the audio driver at real-time priority and keep the machine idle.

How we know. Live simulation (live/run.sh timing): 109 missed periods, 218 ms behind; 0 with SCHED_FIFO. Live-path simulation: the real audioIO/RtAudio ASIO code built with GCC on Linux and driven by a fake ASIO driver; rates are indicative, not Windows-exact. Audit notes

LIVE-8 Low D

Live onset and offset ramps are a 500 Hz sawtooth and end on a negative gain

What happens. With trialLen and rampLen set, the live ramp gain is computed from an index that runs over the interleaved stereo buffer, so within each 2 ms frame the ramp advances twice as fast and then jumps back. The gain is a 500 Hz sawtooth of ±0.040 around the intended ramp and ends at −0.039.

When it matters. Audible only if speech overlaps the first or last rampLen of a trial.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Compute the ramp from the frame's sample index, not the interleaved index.

How we know. Live simulation (live/run.sh ramp): live vs offline gain, maximum difference 0.040, final live gain −0.039. Live-path simulation: the real audioIO/RtAudio ASIO code built with GCC on Linux and driven by a fake ASIO driver; rates are indicative, not Windows-exact. Audit notes

Robustness

Memory reads and writes past the end of an array, and similar defects that need a malformed file or parameter, or an unusual build, to show up. None changes what a participant hears with well-formed settings; each is worth fixing because the failure, when it happens, is silent or a crash.

OST-F4

Medium severity

  • H Harness
  • D Driver

Audit notes
Findings log

A PCF with fewer rows than the OST has states makes Audapter read past its arrays, and memory contents decide whether formants are shifted

Not triggered: blab's PCFs have one row per OST state. Affects any PCF with fewer rows than the OST has states.
Relevant blab studies safe as run. Safe as run: blab's PCFs have one row per OST state.

What happens

The formant path indexes the PCF's amplitude and phase arrays with the current OST state without checking the PCF's length. In OST states beyond the PCF's last row, it reads whatever lies after the arrays in memory, and that value decides whether and how much to shift.

When it matters

Affects OST/PCF pairs where the PCF has fewer rows than the OST has states, which the file format allows and the loader does not check, for example a PCF written only up to the last perturbed state. Pitch and intensity shifts check the length and are not affected. What happens depends on memory contents, which differ between machines and sessions.

Example

An OST with states 0–4 and a 3-row PCF that raises F1 in state 2. From 0.39 s, in states 3 and 4, every frame (404 of 600) reads past the 12-byte arrays; AddressSanitizer stops at the first read. In this Linux run the bytes read were zero, so no extra frames were shifted; on another machine they need not be.

No recordings: the effect depends on memory contents, so any clip would be one arbitrary instance.

How big, how often

syntheticFrames reading past the arrays404 of 600 (67 %), from 0.39 s
syntheticAllocated / largest index read12 bytes (3 entries) / state 4
syntheticShifted frames outside state 2, this run0

Data: data.json from the export script.

Cause

PERT_CFG::readFromFile allocates one entry per PCF row. handleBuffer indexes the formant arrays with the OST state and checks only that the PCF is not empty.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Safe pattern and fix

Check stat < pertCfg.n in the formant path, as the pitch path does, and reject at load a PCF with fewer rows than the OST has states. Workaround: always write one PCF row per OST state.

How we know

  • H sanitizer scenario (build-asan): t_mem.m SCEN=pcf_short heap-buffer-overflow READ at Audapter.cpp:1811, 0 bytes after an 8-byte region allocated at pcf.cpp:431
  • H report export (ASan run + timeline): report_ost_f4.m run under build-asan first (log to out/report/ost-f4/asan.log), then on build-oct
  • D standalone driver of pcf.cpp: scratch/ost-pcf/t/drvp.cpp oob PCF n = 5: fmtPertAmp[6] = 4.6e-44 (during_trans = 1), fmtPertPhi[8] = 4.3e18

Reproduce cd audit/harness && SCEN=pcf_short ./run-oct.sh t_mem.m build-asan

FMT-F1

Medium severity

  • H Harness

Audit notes
Findings log

A clamp trajectory shorter than 2048 values is read as 2048: after it ends, the formant clamp follows whatever lies next in memory

Not triggered by blab's public code, which does no formant clamping; the settings of blab's clamping experiment were not available to us. Affects clamp trajectories shorter than 2048 values.
Relevant blab studies safe as run. Safe as run: taimComp pads its clamp trajectories to 2048 values.

What happens

The setters for clampf1/clampf2 copy 2048 values whatever length MATLAB passes, so a shorter trajectory is followed by memory contents. The clamp runs on into those values until it meets a zero. The 1D-field arrays behave the same way with 257 values.

When it matters

Affects clamped-formant experiments whose trajectories are shorter than 2048 values; the default parameters pad to 2048 and are safe. The values read past the array vary from run to run and between machines, so the effect ranges from harmless to a formant pushed to 0 Hz.

Example

A 100-value trajectory at 700 Hz on a vowel. Audapter copies 2048 values, 1948 of them from past MATLAB's array. In this run the clamp followed the 100 values, then memory values until the first zero at element 104, and held a target of 1.15e-312 Hz: F1 pushed to 0 Hz, and the output peaked at 628 times full scale, a peak 75 dB above the padded control's.

Cause

In set mode, setGetParam uses maxNClampFrames (2048) as the copy length for the clamp arrays whatever length MATLAB passed. The zero-fill of the rest is commented out. The 1D-field arrays use a fixed 257.

Introduced in the blab-lab fork.

Safe pattern and fix

In set mode copy min(nPars, max) values and zero the rest; better, reject arrays of the wrong length. Workaround: always pad clamp trajectories to 2048 values and field arrays to 257.

How we know

Further robustness items

I-06 / I-07 Medium H

An oversized tone count is accepted and overwrites neighbouring parameters

What happens. The tsgNTones range check reads the value before it is assigned, so 100 is accepted although the maximum is 64. The next tone-sequence setter then writes past the tone arrays into neighbouring parameters (stereoMode, bShift2D, clamp settings). The tone-sequence recorder also has no bound and overruns after 10 s.

When it matters. Affects scripts that set more than 64 tones or play tone sequences longer than 10 s.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Check the new value, not the old one, and bound the recorder.

How we know. Harness (scratch/interface/t_iface.m T5) for the check order; the overflow by reading. Audit notes

OST-F6 Medium D

Reloading an OST file that has no maxIOI section crashes MATLAB

What happens. Loading a new OST frees the maxIOI arrays. If the new file has no maxIOI section, the parser returns without setting their count to 0, and the next frame dereferences the freed arrays.

When it matters. Affects sessions that load one OST with a maxIOI section and then one without; gen_multi_pert_pcf.m writes files without it.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Set maxIOICfg.n = 0 before returning. Workaround: always end OST files with an n = 0 maxIOI section.

How we know. Standalone ost.cpp driver (scratch/ost-pcf/t): segfault on the first frame after the reload. Audit notes

H2 / PT-1 Low H F

The first output frame of each trial, and one frame every 108 s, is read from outside the delay buffer

What happens. The read position in the output delay ring uses > 0 where >= 0 is needed. When the write position minus the delay is exactly 0, the frame is read past the end of the buffer. The pitch-shift "back zeroing" on the same ring can also write before the start of the buffer.

When it matters. The read happens at frame delayFrames of every trial and once per 108 s lap. At a trial start the wrongly read frame is near-silent, so it is benign; in continuous sessions longer than 108 s without a reset it gives a 2 ms glitch. The back-zeroing write happens only with pitch shifting when the write position is below delayFrames·frameLen + pvocHop.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Use >= 0 in the read-pointer test and a positive modulo in the back zeroing; both are proven to stay in bounds for every setting and to address the same samples wherever the original was valid.

How we know. UBSan reports the read on every harness run (Audapter.cpp:2124). CBMC on the verbatim source gives the exact conditions and proves both fixes. Audit notes

COORD-5 Low H R

A rejected time-warp row terminates the process on Linux, macOS and WebAssembly builds (portability)

What happens. PERT_CFG::addWarpCfg declares that it throws only overlappingWarpIntervalsError, but it also throws warpCfgInitError when a warp rate is outside its range (rate1 not in (0, 1), or rate2 not above 1). GCC and clang enforce the declaration and terminate the process; MSVC ignores it, so on the lab's Windows rigs MATLAB reports "Failed to initialize time-warping event" instead.

When it matters. Not a crash on Windows. It matters for Linux, macOS and browser builds, and for anyone who writes a rate-1 warp row to mean "no warp": that row is rejected rather than treated as a no-op. Use a zero-length warp row instead.

Present since at least Audapter 2.1.5.

Fix. Drop the dynamic exception specification (it is deprecated since C++11), or declare both exception types.

How we know. Harness: a PCF warp row with rate 1 (a "null warp") terminated Octave on Linux; reading of the exception specification. Audit notes

Methods

Running the real code without MATLAB or audio hardware

The C++ core is compiled as a MEX file for GNU Octave, which implements MATLAB's MEX interface, and driven through the lab's own MATLAB code (getAudapterDefaultParams.m, AudapterIO.m), unmodified. Audio goes in frame by frame through Audapter('runFrame'), which runs the same processing function as the live audio callback. We then read back what Audapter logged and measured the output audio independently: formants with our own LPC, F0 by autocorrelation, and level in 20 ms blocks. The only source changes are two portability edits, one of which makes GCC behave like the Windows compiler. A second build with AddressSanitizer and UBSan reports out-of-bounds memory access at the exact line.

Checks on the test setup

  • Repeated identical trials give bit-identical output, and the tracker agrees with an independent LPC within 5 % on four vowels.
  • An apparent 25 % overshoot of F1 shifts at F0 200 Hz was a bias of our LPC measurement: vowels synthesised at the target formant show the same bias. Formant checks use F0 120 Hz.
  • We ran the original Audapter 2.1.5 through the same harness, on synthetic input and on the real recordings. Output and logged data matched bit for bit, except for the field re-entry rule in F6.
  • The WebAssembly build matches a native build with the same maths library bit for bit, and the MATLAB-compiled build within 3·10−11.

Real speech

Every main finding was repeated on 80 openly licensed recordings (197 s): adult men and women, children aged 6–7, singers, voices with dysphonia, speech in real background noise, and three session recordings shipped with Audapter. A script re-fetches each original from pinned sources and rebuilds the set byte for byte. On these recordings the formant tracker's median error against the hand-corrected measurements of Hillenbrand et al. (1995) is 1.3–2.0 %; formant shifts are logged exactly and measured in the output within 2–3 % of the command; the old sessions replay within 0.2–0.4 % of what was logged online; and the sanitizers found nothing new in 480 clip-scenarios. No voice in the set is above about 350 Hz F0, so high voices are untested.

The live audio path

To test the path used in experiments, the real audio code (audioIO.cpp and RtAudio with its ASIO backend) was built with Audapter and driven by a simulated ASIO driver that calls back at real period boundaries, and cross-checked against a JACK server. Live processing matches offline processing bit for bit, with two buffers of delay, so the offline cards apply to real sessions. The usual reset–start–stop–getData flow per trial showed no data races in 300 runs under ThreadSanitizer. The driver is modelled and the build is GCC on Linux, so crash and click rates are indicative, not Windows figures.

Proofs

For a few pieces of logic we asked for which settings a bug occurs and whether the fix works for all settings. CBMC, a model checker for C, runs on the verbatim, hash-pinned buffer-index code and was checked for every frame length Audapter accepts (1–120) and six common larger ones, with no failures. It gives the exact conditions for the delay-buffer and recorder overruns and proves their fixes. Lean 4 proves, on a line-by-line model of the OST state machine, that with the OST-F1 and OST-F2 fixes no trial depends on earlier trials, and that neither fix alone suffices; the proof is about the model, not the compiled code. Exact algebra gives the phase vocoder's 3/2 gain (PT-5) for every hop ratio of 3 or more. The whole signal-processing chain was not model-checked.

Running Audapter in the browser

Panels on several cards run the real C++ core, compiled to WebAssembly from the same commit, on the card's inputs, with and without a small patch. Each patch is bit-identical to the current code on reference scenarios it should not affect and removes the finding's effect (audit/report/wasm/check-patches.mjs). Panels load on click, work offline, and use 150–300 MB of memory per run; on a phone, run one panel at a time.

Who did this, and reproducing it

The audit was carried out by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, with AI sub-agents, at the request of Josh Mandel, who commissioned it and decided what to publish. Nothing here needs to be taken on trust: every finding links the code at a pinned commit and gives a reproduce command. The whole pipeline was rebuilt from a fresh clone; of the 17 full cards the report then had, 13 rebuilt byte-identical, and the other 4 measure quantities that vary by nature (a click's size, crash counts, time to a hang, memory contents). Requires Docker: ./reproduce.sh at the repository root rebuilds everything.

Running the lab's own code

To check findings against the experiments as the lab runs them, we ran each public blab experiment's own entry script, runner and shared helpers, unmodified, under Octave with the real Audapter build behind a virtual sound card on a virtual clock (pause and timers advance the recording instead of waiting), with a participant who says each trial's word or sentence and a rule-driven experimenter answering prompts and dialogs through their real callbacks. Per trial it records every Audapter call, the parameters in effect against the script's own, the OST timeline, the logged shift and the heard formants, pitch, level and lag. 12 of the 13 public entry points run end to end (vsaCentralize's stops because the runner it calls is not in its repository); vsaGeneralize and the modelExpt template ran full sessions. The participant is one of eight AI-generated voices (OpenAI text to speech, four perceived female and four male; every take checked for what was said, clipping, F0 and vowel formants, and checked against real recordings of "head"), each running every experiment; the numbers quoted from these runs are their range across the eight voices. Participant setup is simulated too: the experimenter answers the height question from the voice's gender (the male or female preset) and, where the script opens the lab's LPC check, tries every order the tool offers through the tool itself and keeps the preset unless another order is clearly and consistently better on formant accuracy against an independent reference, track continuity and vowel clustering (the rule was fixed before it was run; it kept the preset in almost every session). Limits: AI-generated voices are studio-clean renditions, not people; no real-time scheduling or sound-card timing, simplified Psychtoolbox, and one recorded load-time change (graphics dot notation) in files that fail without it. Details: audit/labrun/README.md.

Level and loudness

Cards state level changes as A-weighted level differences, in dBA: 20·log10 of the ratio of the A-weighted RMS of two clips, measured on the output audio over the part of the signal the card names (for whole clips, the 20 ms blocks within 40 dB of the loudest). A-weighting (IEC 61672) discounts low and very high frequencies roughly as the ear does at moderate levels; it is standard and needs no assumption about the listening level. The plain, unweighted RMS level overstates changes that mostly move energy at low frequencies: lowering F1, for example, boosts the strong low harmonics, to which the ear is less sensitive, so on the ARCTIC bdl sentence F1 −125 mel raises the plain RMS level by 6.7 dB but the A-weighted level by 2.9 dBA. Plain RMS appears only in evidence tables, labelled RMS. For /s/ and other broadband changes the measures agree closely.

Where a card compares clips we also give the loudness-level difference in phon (ISO 532-1): ISO 532-1 time-varying loudness (Zwicker; mosqito 1.2.1, free field), statistic N5 (the loudness exceeded 5 % of the time), converted to loudness level. The expected clip is presented at 60, 70, 80 and 85 dB SPL (A-weighted), the observed clip at the same gain, and the card gives the range over those levels; we assume diotic headphones with a flat response and a normal-hearing listener. Older or clinical listeners and real headphones may differ. For "noticeable" we use a change of about 1 dB (about 1 phon at these levels), the order of the intensity just-noticeable difference for broadband sounds such as speech and noise at moderate levels (Miller 1947, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 19:609). Sanity check (equal RMS, +2 semitones, 70 dB SPL): a harmonic complex at 120 Hz gains +0.4 phon, the direction the equal-loudness contours predict.

Limitations

  • Octave, not MATLAB; GCC on Linux, not MSVC on Windows. Out-of-bounds reads can return different values on Windows.
  • The live path is simulated with a modelled ASIO driver.
  • Recordings, not a live talker hearing the feedback; no voices above about 350 Hz F0.
  • Severity is our judgement of experimental impact.
